title: In Profile: Anna Wallace, CEO at CFIT
snippet: CFIT chief executive Anna Wallace on moving fintech out of the pilot stage, a sandbox idea that came too early and the trust questions agentic payments raise. The post In Profile: Anna Wallace, CEO at CFIT appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Anna Wallace has spent more than two decades where regulation, policy and financial innovation meet. At the Financial Conduct Authority she led the world’s first regulatory sandbox, she later worked on financial inclusion at the Gates Foundation, and she is now chief executive of the Centre for Finance, Innovation and Technology (CFIT).

Anna Wallace, CEO at CFIT

CFIT was set up after the 2021 Kalifa Review of UK Fintech to bring industry, regulators, government and technologists together on problems no single organisation can solve alone. Its coalitions have covered Open Finance, Digital Company ID, SME access to finance, Open Property and, most recently, Supported Payments.

In this In Profile, Anna Wallace, CEO at CFIT, discusses moving good ideas out of pilots and into the market, the cross-sector sandbox that came too early, and the trust questions raised by agentic payments.

Tell us more about your company and its purpose

The Centre for Finance, Innovation and Technology (CFIT) was established following the 2021 Kalifa Review of UK Fintech to bring together the organisations needed to tackle systemic challenges that no single part of the market can solve alone.

As a neutral convener, we create time-bound coalitions spanning financial services, technology, government, regulators, standards bodies and other relevant parts of the ecosystem. But our role goes beyond convening stakeholders or producing recommendations.

Our coalitions are designed to move from identifying a shared challenge to developing, building and testing practical solutions, including prototypes and minimum viable products, alongside the trust, governance, legal and policy frameworks needed to support their adoption.

We’ve applied that model to Open Finance, Digital Company ID, SME access to finance, Open Property and, most recently, financial inclusion through Supported Payments.

Ultimately, it’s about helping turn good ideas into practical change. By testing solutions with real market participants and generating evidence about what works, we can give industry and Government greater confidence that new approaches are not only technically possible, but trusted, commercially viable and capable of being implemented at scale.

What are some of your recent achievements you’d like to highlight?

We’ve made significant progress over the past year across several different challenges.

Our Digital Company ID Coalition developed an MVP enabling effective data exchange between SMEs, identity data providers and banks, which was accepted into the Financial Conduct Authority’s Regulatory Sandbox.

Our SME Access to Finance Coalition tested two financial health tools, a Funding Health Checker and Small Business Coach, and identified changes that could potentially unlock around £5 billion in additional SME lending.

Building on our first Coalition on Open Finance, we also published our Open Property Roadmap, providing a blueprint for applying Smart Data principles beyond financial services to help digitise the homebuying process. We’re now moving that work from roadmap to implementation, bringing together organisations from across the property ecosystem to develop and test practical solutions.

Most recently, in partnership with Project Nemo and Her Majesty Queen Máxima of the Netherlands, we launched our fifth national Coalition, focused initially on developing a Supported Payments framework. The aim is to help people who need assistance managing their finances make everyday payments safely while retaining greater independence and control.

How did you get into the fintech industry?

I had a relatively conventional route into fintech. I studied Philosophy, Politics and Economics at university and had always been interested in financial services, particularly how it can be transformed to make it work better for people.

That led me to the FCA, where I became Head of Innovation and led the world’s first regulatory sandbox, as well as work to establish new approaches to cross-border regulatory collaboration. I also commissioned the first Bank of England and FCA survey into machine learning in financial services in 2019.

After nine transformative years at the FCA, I joined the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation as a Senior Programme Officer, working on financial inclusion.

Now I’m in my first CEO role at CFIT, which gives me an opportunity to bring together those experiences across finance, technology, regulation, innovation and inclusion to help unlock growth and tackle challenges across a range of industries.

What’s the best thing about working in the fintech industry?

For me, it’s the ability to use financial innovation to unlock change across so many different parts of the economy. Fintech isn’t only about financial services: we’re increasingly seeing its principles and technologies applied to areas such as property, energy and retail.

It’s also one of those industries where technical innovation and human impact come together very directly. Whether it’s changing how somebody makes a payment, helping a small business access finance or making it easier to buy a home, the technology can have a tangible effect on people’s everyday lives.

And it never really stops. There are always new ideas, technologies and challenges emerging. That’s what makes it such an exciting industry to work in.

What frustrates you most about the fintech industry?

We have no shortage of innovation, but we can still be too slow at getting good ideas out of pilots and into the market at scale.

Often that’s because the organisations needed to make something work (banks, technology providers, government, regulators and others) are operating in different parts of the system. Even where everyone agrees on the opportunity, issues such as standards, governance, liability or commercial incentives can prevent progress.

We won’t solve genuinely systemic challenges if everyone works independently. That’s particularly important as areas such as AI and tokenisation develop rapidly and international competition intensifies.

It’s one of the reasons CFIT exists. Our role is to create a neutral environment where those different organisations can collaborate, test solutions and generate the evidence needed to give the market confidence to move from innovation to adoption.

How have your previous roles influenced your career?

I’ve been lucky enough to look at innovation through three very different lenses: government, regulation and investment.

Government taught me to think about impact at scale: what needs to change across a whole system, rather than for one organisation. At the FCA, I learnt that regulation can be an enabler of innovation, but also that you have to understand risk, consumer outcomes and what makes change possible in practice. And working as an investor at the Gates Foundation gave me another perspective again: being really disciplined about where you put resources, what will genuinely move the dial and how you measure impact.

Those different lenses have shaped how I approach CFIT today. I’m always interested in the innovation itself, but equally in the system around it: what Government needs, what regulators need, what makes the commercial case stack up and, ultimately, whether it will make a meaningful difference to people and businesses.

What’s the best mistake you’ve ever made?

Probably being too early on an idea.

At the FCA in 2019, I led work exploring a cross-sector regulatory sandbox, essentially asking whether businesses developing innovations that crossed regulatory boundaries should have a way of working with multiple regulators together.

It didn’t really take off. I think the market, and probably the regulatory system, wasn’t quite ready for it.

But the problem we identified was real. Today, the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum is bringing regulators together around technologies and issues that cut across traditional boundaries, and at CFIT we repeatedly see innovations, whether AI, digital identity or Smart Data, that don’t fit neatly within one regulator’s remit.

So the mistake wasn’t identifying the problem. It was probably underestimating how long systems take to become ready for an idea.

It’s taught me not to confuse “not now” with “not right”. Sometimes you need to keep hold of an idea until the conditions catch up with it.

What has the future got in store for your company?

We’re always looking at where collaboration can unlock the next wave of progress.

A particular focus is on areas where there is already significant innovation, but where systemic barriers are preventing that innovation from moving beyond individual pilots or products and reaching scale. That could include agentic commerce, tokenisation, wealthtech infrastructure or applying Smart Data principles to sectors such as energy and transport.

Our previous Coalitions have shown what a coordinated approach can achieve. Increasingly, our focus is not simply on identifying opportunities or producing recommendations, but on helping industry move from alignment to implementation: developing, building and testing practical solutions and creating the evidence needed for adoption.

There is a significant prize if we can get that right: faster adoption, lower system costs, better outcomes for consumers and businesses, and ultimately a more competitive and innovative UK economy.

What are the next key talking points or challenges for your industry as a whole?

Fraud will remain a major priority, particularly as AI makes fraud more sophisticated and scalable. Deepfakes, synthetic identities and increasingly automated transactions all create new challenges around knowing who, or increasingly what, you are dealing with. Trusted digital identity will therefore become even more important. That’s something we’ve already been exploring through our Digital Company ID work, but the challenge will continue to evolve.

The other area I’m particularly interested in is agentic payments. We’re moving from AI that helps people make decisions towards AI agents that can potentially act and transact on their behalf. That creates enormous opportunities, but also some fundamental questions: how do you identify and authenticate an AI agent? How does a consumer delegate authority to it? Who is liable when something goes wrong? And how do we make sure different agents, institutions and payment systems can interact safely?

The Government’s Financial Services AI Champions, Harriet Rees and Dr Rohit Dhawan, identified this as a priority in their recent AI Adoption Plan. They recommended an industry-led trust framework for agentic payments built around legal and liability frameworks, Know Your Agent protocols, and authentication and governance, with a neutral organisation such as CFIT potentially helping to convene the ecosystem.

That is exactly the kind of systemic challenge where collaboration matters. No bank, technology company or regulator can resolve those questions alone. CFIT can potentially bring together financial institutions, AI companies, payments providers, identity specialists, Government and regulators to develop and test common approaches. The opportunity for the UK is not simply to adopt agentic payments quickly, but to help establish the trusted infrastructure that allows them to scale safely.

The Government has accepted the AI Champions’ recommendations for Government and said it will work with regulators and industry on next steps, so this is likely to become a particularly important area of discussion for the sector.

title: Can Nubank Really Crack the US Market?
snippet: Nubank’s US expansion ambitions and the debate over AI-driven payments highlight two fintech challenges: replicating growth across markets and defining control and liability in agentic commerce. The post Can Nubank Really Crack the US Market? appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Over the past month, Nubank has been making headlines, and it looks increasingly likely that the Brazilian digital banking giant has ambitions beyond Latin America.

In September 2026, Nubank moved closer to entering the US retail banking market through a partnership with Lead Bank. With around 140 million customers globally, it is already the world’s largest digital banking platform by customer base, with roughly twice as many customers as Revolut.

That’s an impressive starting point but cracking the US is another matter.

Nubank has also received conditional approval from the OCC for a US national bank charter, with the aim of securing full approval by 2027. A full charter could give the company greater control over its US operations and a stronger foundation for competing in one of the world’s most lucrative banking markets.

Then came the Monzo rumours.

Reports suggested Nubank could acquire Monzo as part of its European expansion strategy. For Nubank, that would mean an established foothold in the UK. For Monzo, it could bring the financial backing and international reach to revisit its own US ambitions, where earlier expansion efforts struggled to gain traction.

There’s an interesting irony here. Monzo and Revolut were both founded in 2015, with Monzo getting started around five months earlier. Monzo also secured its UK banking licence years before Revolut. Yet Revolut has since built a much broader international business, while Monzo remains more closely tied to its home market.

Could Nubank be the international heavyweight Monzo needs? Perhaps. But Nubank was quick to dismiss the acquisition speculation, saying it had no plans to buy the British digital bank.

I can understand why.

Nubank has built its customer base by focusing on markets it knows. Buying its way into Europe through Monzo might accelerate expansion, but it would also mean taking on another company’s strategy, regulatory challenges and growth ambitions. An acquisition brings scale, but it doesn’t automatically bring success, particularly when Nubank is already working to establish itself in the US.

So where does that leave Nubank?

It has the customer base, the brand recognition and the ambition. But international expansion and replicating success are two very different things.

The US is a crowded market, with established banks, digital challengers and payment companies competing for customers. Acquiring them can be expensive. Getting people to sign up is one thing; convincing them to move their money, make Nubank their primary banking provider and stay for the long term is much harder.

Nubank has already proved it can scale. What it hasn’t yet proved is that its model can travel successfully into a market as competitive and complex as the US.

That’s the real test. Cracking America isn’t simply about adding millions of customers. It’s about turning that growth into a sustainable, profitable business. And 140 million customers elsewhere won’t guarantee that happens.

Jamie Dimon: Get Out of the Way? The Battle for Agentic Payments

I am thoroughly enjoying all the chatter around AI agents and payments. The industry is imagining a world where agents can shop, compare prices, manage subscriptions and make payments on our behalf. It sounds convenient, and the commercial opportunity is enormous.

But there’s a question that deserves just as much attention as the technology itself: when an AI agent gets something wrong, who is liable?

The concern isn’t just that an agent might go off script or be manipulated into making an unauthorised transaction. It’s that responsibility could become increasingly difficult to pin down when the customer, bank, payment provider and company building the agent are all involved.

The US has spent years building safeguards around customer data, privacy, fraud prevention and access to financial accounts. Banks invest heavily in identity verification, transaction monitoring and compliance. Now we’re talking about giving AI agents the ability to act on a customer’s behalf.

The potential is hard to ignore. An agent could compare financial products, negotiate bills, manage subscriptions and find the best way to pay for something. Customers might rarely need to open a banking app.

But convenience comes with a catch. If an agent can access your account and initiate payments, whose interests is it serving? The customer, the bank, the technology company or the merchant trying to make a sale? And if the agent makes a mistake, who picks up the bill?

Banks cannot simply blame the algorithm. Equally, technology companies cannot expect banks to absorb every loss while they control the customer interface.

Banks Are Building Their Own. Is That the Right Move?

Banks are understandably keen to develop their own AI agents. They already have the customer relationships, financial data, regulatory infrastructure and, crucially, access to the money.

Building their own agents gives them greater control over customer information and what those agents can do. It also reduces the risk of technology companies inserting themselves between banks and their customers.

But is building everything in-house really the right strategy?

Banks understand risk, regulation and financial services. That doesn’t automatically make them the best at building consumer AI products or creating the agent ecosystems customers will want to use.

There’s also the risk of fragmentation. If every bank develops its own closed system, we could end up with dozens of competing agents that struggle to work across banks, merchants and payment networks. That hardly sounds like the seamless experience the industry is promising.

And let’s be honest, banks have spent years trying to make their apps easier to use. Now they’re being asked to build systems that understand what customers want, make decisions and potentially move money with limited human intervention.

That’s quite a leap.

The alternative isn’t necessarily better. If independent technology companies become the main interface between customers and their banks, financial institutions risk being pushed into the background. They would still provide the accounts and process the transactions, but someone else could control the customer relationship.

For banks, that’s a serious concern.

The Real Battle Is Over Control

Imagine asking an AI assistant to find the best credit card, compare savings accounts or manage your bills. Rather than opening several banking apps, you tell the agent what you want and let it do the work.

The agent becomes the starting point for the decision. It could influence which financial product you choose, which bank you use and how you pay. The bank might still provide the underlying service, but it could have far less influence over the customer’s choice.

That’s a significant shift in the balance of power.

Payment networks, merchants and technology companies also have a stake in this new layer of commerce. Whoever controls the agent could influence where transactions happen, how payments are routed and which providers are selected.

For years, banks and fintechs have competed to own the customer experience. Agentic AI could put that relationship in the hands of a completely different set of players.

This is no longer just a conversation about chatbots. It’s about who gets to sit between the customer and their money, and who captures the value that comes with it.

The Liability Question

Before agentic payments become mainstream, the industry needs clearer answers on responsibility and control.

Who authorises a payment? Can an agent be restricted to a particular amount, merchant or purpose? What happens if it is compromised? And who is responsible when a transaction goes wrong?

These questions become more complicated when an agent operates across several providers, each with its own systems and obligations.

Existing payment protections still matter, but their application to agent-driven transactions needs careful consideration. Giving an agent permission to make payments doesn’t necessarily mean the customer intended to authorise every transaction it might initiate.

The industry needs to establish clear rules around consent, permissions and responsibility before customers can be expected to trust agents with increasingly consequential financial decisions.

Because if consumers don’t know who is responsible when something goes wrong, convenience will only take the industry so far.

The Next Battle in Payments

I can see why banks want to build their own agents. They have too much at stake to let someone else take control of the customer relationship without a fight.

But building everything in-house may not be the answer either. Agentic commerce will need to work across banks, merchants, payment networks and technology providers. Some level of cooperation will be unavoidable.

The challenge is finding the balance between openness and control: giving agents enough access to be useful without compromising customer security or leaving responsibility unclear.

Financial services have spent years trying to make payments faster, simpler and more secure. Agentic AI could take convenience to another level, but it also raises new questions about consent, accountability and who ultimately controls the transaction.

Banks shouldn’t ignore the opportunity. But neither should they assume that building their own agents will automatically protect their position.

Because the next battle in payments may not be about who moves the money.

It may be about who decides where the money goes.

title: ADIB Launches AED 1.75bn Rights Issue to Fund Vision 2035 Growth
snippet: Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank will issue up to 106 million new shares at AED 16.45, a 28.8% discount, with subscription opening 10 November The post ADIB Launches AED 1.75bn Rights Issue to Fund Vision 2035 Growth appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank (ADIB) has set the key dates for a AED 1.75 billion rights issue following shareholder approval at a general assembly on 6 October 2026 and sign-off from both the Central Bank of the UAE and the Capital Market Authority. The transaction will issue up to 106,383,000 new ordinary shares, lifting the bank’s issued share capital from AED 3.632 billion to up to AED 3.738 billion.

Shareholders registered by the eligibility date of 2 November 2026 will receive one right for every 34.14 existing ADIB shares held. Each right entitles the holder to subscribe for one new share at AED 16.45, comprising a nominal value of AED 1.00 and a share premium of AED 15.45. That price represents a 28.8% discount to ADIB’s closing share price on 24 August 2026. Investors wishing to qualify must execute purchase orders on or before 29 October 2026 to allow for the two-day ADX settlement window.

Rights will trade on the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange (ADX) between 4 and 16 November 2026. The subscription period runs from 10 to 24 November, with new shares expected to begin trading on 18 December 2026. Shareholders who do not exercise their rights may sell them on-market during the trading window, though those who neither exercise nor sell will face percentage ownership dilution once the new shares are listed.

ADIB will act as sole receiving bank for the issue. Subscription channels include the ADX ePortal, participating ADIB branches and the ADIB Mobile App for existing digital banking customers.

Capital strategy and Gulf banking context

Mohamed Abdelbary, group chief executive officer of ADIB, said the bank was entering its next growth phase from a position of strength, with the capital increase designed to pursue opportunities under Vision 2035 while maintaining a robust capital position.

The reference to Vision 2035 aligns the raise with Abu Dhabi’s broader economic diversification agenda, which has driven a sustained expansion in Islamic finance across the emirate. ADIB reported total assets of AED 304 billion as of 30 June 2026, a scale that places it among the largest dedicated Islamic banks globally. The rights issue, while modest relative to total assets, is intended to give the bank headroom to grow its loan book, deepen corporate and private banking relationships, and invest in digital infrastructure without straining its capital adequacy ratios.

Regulatory and market read-across

The dual approval requirement from the Central Bank of the UAE and the Capital Market Authority reflects the layered regulatory architecture that governs listed bank capital raises in the Gulf. The UAE’s banking regulator has historically maintained conservative Tier 1 capital expectations, and a rights issue structured at a clear discount is the conventional tool for ensuring take-up without reliance on underwriters.

The transaction also sits within a broader regional trend. Several Gulf Cooperation Council banks have tapped equity markets in recent years to fund balance sheet growth ahead of anticipated credit demand from government infrastructure programmes and private-sector expansion. For institutional investors already holding ADIB shares, the tradable rights structure preserves optionality: they can subscribe to maintain their stake, sell the right and realise a cash value, or allow dilution if they judge the discount insufficient to justify additional capital allocation. The 28.8% discount is a meaningful incentive designed to minimise the risk of rights trading well below subscription price and discouraging participation.

title: Ramp seeks bank charter
snippet: Ramp applied with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency for a national trust bank charter on Friday.
fullText:
Corporate spend management fintech Ramp applied for a national trust bank charter Friday with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the company wrote Monday in posts on X and LinkedIn.

The company offered few details, saying it would offer fiduciary investment management and digital-asset custody – but would not take deposits or make commercial loans – if the charter is approved. 

“The proposed trust bank would bring these services under a consistent federal regulatory framework, helping us build great products alongside our banking partners to further our mission to save businesses time and money,” the company wrote in its posts.

There has been a competitive rush for charters this year. Block, Avant and Modern Treasury are among the fintechs that have sought OCC charters, all applying over the past two months. They're eager to have access to the Federal Reserve's account and payment rail services.

Ramp’s application was filed just a day after the company announced it had raised $1.85 billion in a financing round led by Dragoneer Investment Group. Ramp is now valued at $60 billion.

The application also comes just weeks after the Independent Community Bankers of America sued the OCC, arguing the recent spike in national trust bank charter applications – and approvals – are creating “a gaping hole in financial regulation.” 

The OCC’s current posture “perversely allow[s] entities engaged in highly risky cryptocurrency and digital assets activities to enter the banking system under lightly regulated national charters rather than the more rigorously regulated traditional bank charter,” which puts community banks at a “severe competitive disadvantage,” the trade group asserted in its lawsuit, filed Oct. 2.

The OCC has approved, or conditionally approved, 21 national trust bank charters since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, the ICBA noted. Thirteen of those have come from crypto companies, the trade group said.

“There is no statutory basis for the OCC’s position that it can charter crypto trust banks that are neither depository nor fiduciary,” the ICBA argued in its lawsuit.

Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould, however, has defended his agency’s conditional charter approvals, saying “we don’t have a zero risk tolerance anymore.”

“That’s not what the statute says. The statute talks about a reasonable chance of success. That’s how we evaluate applications,” Gould said at an event in May. 

Ji Hun Kim, CEO of trade association Crypto Council for Innovation, said ICBA’s lawsuit “is a clear attempt to resist national trust charters, payments innovation, and competition in financial services.”

“Restricting banking to legacy business models will not stop demand for financial innovation,” Kim said this month. 

Ramp, for its part, has solidified its leadership this year, naming co-founder Karim Atiyeh, previously the company’s chief technology officer, as co-CEO, alongside co-founder Eric Glyman.

Additionally, Ramp tapped Rahul Sengottuvelu, previously its head of applied artificial intelligence, to become its next tech chief. Before joining Ramp, Sengottuvelu served as CTO at Cohere, which Ramp bought in 2023.

title: Loops Raises $3.5m Seed to Unify AI Commerce Tools for Retailers
snippet: The San Francisco startup closed a $3.5m seed round led by a16z Speedrun to build a single AI layer covering search, discovery and customer The post Loops Raises $3.5m Seed to Unify AI Commerce Tools for Retailers appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Loops, a San Francisco-based commerce AI startup, has closed a $3.5 million seed round from a16z Speedrun, NTT Docomo, Connecticut Innovations, Alumni Ventures and Monday Capital. The company is building what it positions as a unified AI operating layer for retailers, replacing the patchwork of point solutions that most e-commerce businesses currently assemble across search, product discovery, shopping assistance, catalogue enrichment and virtual try-on.

The funding will support product development, customer deployment capacity and international expansion, according to the company.

The consolidation thesis

Ilker Selim Zorluoglu, co-Founder & president at Loops

The core argument Loops is making is structural rather than feature-level. Most retailers that have adopted AI have done so one workflow at a time: a search upgrade here, a chatbot there, a catalogue-writing tool somewhere else. Each system carries only partial context about the shopper and the product inventory, creating seams in the customer journey that erode conversion.

Loops says it addresses that by building all the components on a shared layer that holds the retailer’s catalogue data, business context and the shopper’s in-session intent simultaneously. The claim is that improvements in one module reinforce the others: richer catalogue data sharpens search results, better search gives the shopping assistant more accurate context, and customer conversations surface gaps in product information.

Ilker Selim Zorluoglu, president and co-founder, said: “A retailer does not need five different AI products that each understand one slice of the customer. It needs one system that understands the catalog, the business and what the shopper is trying to do.”

The company reports over 70 customers and pilots. Turkish supermarket chain A101 and fashion retailer Mavi are named customers. Loops says sessions on A101’s platform involving its tools showed roughly 83% higher observed purchase conversion compared with a non-platform segment, though it acknowledges the figure is observational and not derived from a randomised controlled test. Separately, the company says 64% of pilots have converted into paying customers.

Fareed Mosavat, investment partner at a16z Speedrun, pointed to that pilot conversion rate as evidence of demand. “Loops is starting in commerce, where the link between a better AI experience and business value is unusually clear,” he said.

Market context and competitive landscape

The retail AI consolidation thesis is not unique to Loops. Several well-capitalised players, including established commerce platform vendors and dedicated AI search providers, are pursuing similar integration strategies. Algolia, Bloomreach and Coveo have each expanded their offerings beyond search toward broader personalisation and discovery suites. Adobe and Salesforce have embedded AI assistants into their commerce clouds. The distinguishing factor Loops is staking out is the depth of cross-module integration and the avoidance of a general-purpose model wrapper, which it argues is insufficient for the operational complexity of real retail businesses.

The go-to-market context matters here. Selling a unified platform to retailers is a longer and more complex sales cycle than selling a point solution. Retailers with existing contracts across multiple vendors face integration and switching costs, and procurement decisions of this kind often stall at the IT and data-governance layer before they reach the commerce team. Loops will need to demonstrate that the productivity and conversion gains justify the displacement of incumbent tools, a case that becomes more persuasive as the observational data matures into auditable results.

Beyond commerce, Loops has flagged financial services and energy as the next sectors it intends to address with the same architecture, building what it describes as industry-specific AI operating systems. The expansion is at an early stage, and the company has not disclosed a timeline or named partners in either vertical. The commercial logic is clear enough: if the platform approach proves durable in retail, the same model could command significant enterprise value in regulated sectors where context and compliance requirements make general-purpose AI less viable. The seed funding, at $3.5 million, is modest relative to that ambition, so a Series A timeline and the metrics that will underpin it are the next signals to watch.

title: OKX UAE Launches Tokenised US Stocks with 24/7 Trading on VARA Licence
snippet: OKX UAE is offering over 80 tokenised US stocks to eligible users in Dubai, with AED funding and round-the-clock trading under its VARA The post OKX UAE Launches Tokenised US Stocks with 24/7 Trading on VARA Licence appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
OKX UAE, the Dubai-regulated arm of global digital-assets platform OKX, has launched more than 80 tokenised US stocks for eligible UAE users, giving them price exposure to major technology and AI companies around the clock, including weekends and outside conventional Wall Street trading hours. The product is live from 12 October 2026.

The offering is structured as a real-world asset product: users receive 1:1 price exposure to the underlying equity, can build fractional positions, and are entitled to the economic benefit of eligible dividends. Crucially, the stocks sit within the same OKX app as digital-assets holdings, funded directly by UAE bank accounts in dirhams. AED deposits and withdrawals are near-instant and carry no fees, a detail likely designed to reduce friction for retail and semi-institutional investors who hold cash locally but want exposure to US-listed equities.

OKX UAE operates under a licence from the Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA) and holds VASP reference VL/23/12/003. VARA’s framework, which covers exchange, management, investment, broker-dealer, and lending services, is one of the more detailed virtual-asset licensing regimes in the Gulf, and it is the regulatory foundation that makes the cross-asset product commercially feasible in this jurisdiction.

The RWA context

Rifad Mahasneh, CEO at OKX MENA

Rifad Mahasneh, chief executive of OKX MENA and CIS, said: “By bringing exposure to leading US companies and major indices onchain through tokenised stocks, we’re showing traditional investors how crypto-native infrastructure can enable 24/7 trading, and a more flexible way to access global markets.”

The launch sits within a broader wave of real-world asset tokenisation that has gained traction across institutional and retail fintech in 2025 and 2026. Several platforms, including Backed Finance and others operating out of European and Gulf jurisdictions, have pursued RWA tokenisation of equities and fixed-income instruments, each navigating a patchwork of national securities and virtual-asset regimes. What distinguishes the OKX UAE approach is scale: 80-plus stocks at launch, a large existing user base, and the full-spectrum VARA licence rather than a narrower approval.

The RWA segment is also drawing regulatory attention beyond the Gulf. The EU’s MiCA framework, which came into full effect in December 2024, does not directly govern tokenised equities, which remain under MiFID II. That distinction matters because platforms distributing these products cross-border must carefully delineate between virtual-asset regulation and securities regulation. OKX’s disclaimer explicitly excludes US residents, a standard precaution given SEC scrutiny of tokenised securities offered to American retail investors.

What comes next

OKX told investors in August that the platform traded $680 billion in a single month, and Bloomberg reported earlier this year that Standard Chartered and Circle participated in a funding round at a $25 billion valuation. That capital position, if confirmed at close, would give OKX substantial runway to build out regulated product lines across multiple jurisdictions simultaneously.

For the UAE, the tokenised-stock launch is consistent with the country’s wider strategy of positioning Dubai and Abu Dhabi as competitive financial centres by combining a permissive but structured digital-asset regime with access to global markets. The measure of success here will be adoption data: whether UAE-based investors, many of whom already hold US equities through conventional brokers, shift activity onto an onchain platform in meaningful volumes, and whether OKX can eventually extend the model to Gulf Cooperation Council equities and other regional indices.

title: Ziina Secures Triple CBUAE Licensing Across Payments, Stored Value, and Exchange
snippet: Ziina becomes the first UAE fintech to secure CBUAE licenses across retail payments, stored value, and exchange, enabling unified digital wallets, merchant acquiring, and cross-border transfers. The post Ziina Secures Triple CBUAE Licensing Across Payments, Stored Value, and Exchange appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
In a significant regulatory milestone for the Middle Eastern fintech ecosystem, consumer and enterprise financial platform Ziina has secured its Retail Payment Services Category III license and gained regulatory authorization to conduct Exchange Business Category IV activities from the Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE). With these approvals, Ziina becomes the first homegrown UAE financial technology company to hold regulatory permissions spanning stored value facilities, retail payment services, and digital currency exchange.

The dual authorization marks the completion of Ziina’s phased licensing trajectory with the CBUAE, providing the company with an independent regulatory perimeter to operate a comprehensive financial platform. By combining these authorizations into a unified infrastructure, Ziina can offer an integrated suite of services—spanning consumer deposits, merchant acceptance, domestic real-time settlement, and cross-border money transfers—within a single proprietary application layer.

A Unified Three-Pillar Regulatory Architecture

Faisal Toukan, co-founder and CEO of Ziina

Rather than relying on third-party sponsorship or fragmented intermediary partnerships, Ziina’s newly expanded licensing structure gives the company direct regulatory oversight across three core operational pillars:

Stored Value Facility (SVF): Originally granted by the CBUAE in June 2024, the SVF license authorizes the firm to hold customer balances, operate digital wallets, and safeguard fiat funds.

Retail Payment Services (Category III): Expands the platform’s merchant acquiring, payment aggregation, and domestic fund transfer capabilities. The license provides regulatory authorization for Ziina’s commercial acceptance tools, including online payment gateways, customizable payment links, QR code transactions, and soft-POS Tap to Pay functionality across iOS and Android devices.

Exchange Business (Category IV): Formally authorized under its SVF framework in August 2026, this permission allows Ziina to facilitate international money transfers and multi-currency foreign exchange digitally, enabling users to remit funds cross-border directly through the Ziina app.

“We’re thankful for the continued support of the Central Bank of the UAE,” stated Faisal Toukan, co-founder and CEO of Ziina. “These licenses give us the regulatory framework to build faster and go further. When we launched Ziina in the UAE, we believed that we could build the next generation of financial products from this market, for the region. Today, people use different apps and providers for different parts of their financial lives. We want to bring more financial services into one platform, from spending and holding money to sending it abroad. Our ambition is to take what we build here to enable financial freedom across the Arab world.”

Commercial Scale and SME Market Penetration

Founded in 2020 by Faisal Toukan, Sarah Toukan, and Talal Toukan, Ziina has evolved from a peer-to-peer mobile payments provider into a critical operational engine for the UAE business sector. The platform currently serves more than 500,000 active retail and enterprise customers annually and processes over $1.5 billion in annualized transaction volume.

Significantly, the platform is now utilized by one in ten small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) across the UAE, supported by its transparent pricing model and native merchant features such as the Ziina Card (compatible with Apple Pay and Google Pay) and the Ziina Violet lifestyle membership offering fee-free foreign transactions.

Capitalizing on UAE Digital Payment Velocity

Ziina’s expanded regulatory status coincides with rapid growth across the UAE’s domestic payment infrastructure. According to the CBUAE’s Annual Report 2025, retail fund transfers executed through the UAE Funds Transfer System (UAEFTS) reached AED 9.9 trillion across 114.9 million transactions in 2025. This represents an annual increase of 19.9 per cent in total transaction value and 17.8 per cent in transaction volume, reflecting an accelerating regional migration toward cashless rails and instant digital settlement.

By combining direct regulatory licensing with full-stack merchant and consumer capabilities, Ziina is establishing a scalable blueprint to capture regional market share as digital payments, commercial acquiring, and international remittances continue to consolidate into unified platforms across the Arab world.

title: Northern FinTech Summit 2026: Trust Takes Centre Stage as Sector Tackles AI, Risk and Growth
snippet: FinTech North's Northern FinTech Summit 2026 in York put trust at the heart of discussions on AI, cybersecurity, financial inclusion and skills. The post Northern FinTech Summit 2026: Trust Takes Centre Stage as Sector Tackles AI, Risk and Growth appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
From AI agents making financial decisions to geopolitical threats, financial inclusion and the future of work, day one of FinTech North‘s Northern FinTech Summit 2026 in York showed just how many of the sector’s challenges come down to ‘trust’.

York’s Guildhall has seen plenty over the centuries. Built in 1445, it has hosted council meetings and criminal trials, and is thought to be where a £200,000 ransom for King Charles I was counted out.

On Wednesday, money was still on the agenda as FinTech North returned to the city for the first day of its Northern FinTech Summit 2026. This time, the discussion included whether AI agents could end up triggering bank runs while we’re asleep.

The possibility was raised by Colin Payne, head of innovation at the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), during the opening Chris Sier Keynote, delivered in memory of FinTech North’s former chairman.

Payne warned that a ‘swarm of agents’ all making financial decisions at once could cause serious problems, especially when they’re acting faster than any human can keep track of. AI agents can already pay bills, negotiate with suppliers and manage everyday tasks on our behalf.

He described what he called a ‘trust inversion’ – we’ve got the technology, but how many of us are ready to let an AI agent loose on our bank accounts?

“The technology is here now. It’s arriving before consumers have got trust in it,” he warned.

Payne brought up George Hudson, York’s ‘Railway King’, who helped put the city on the railway map before things went rather badly wrong. In 1849, it turned out Hudson had been paying dividends using investors’ capital rather than profits. Not quite what the people putting their money into the railways had signed up for.

Payne reckons there’s a lesson in that for AI. The railways were booming before anyone had got a proper grip on how they were being run. Now we’ve got AI agents that can manage our money and make decisions for us, while regulators and businesses are still working out who takes responsibility when something goes wrong, or how anyone is supposed to keep track of it all.

That doesn’t mean Payne wants to put the brakes on AI. “Doing nothing is a risk as well,” he said, suggesting that the North’s fintech community has an opportunity to help drive what comes next and make sure people can trust it.

Trust under pressure

Trust was turning into something of a word of the day at the Guildhall, although it meant different things to different speakers.

For Ben Wilson, vice president of government affairs and policy at Mastercard, it was about keeping financial systems secure at a time when geopolitical tensions were creating more risks for businesses.

“Trust is the most valuable asset here,” he said, warning that even fintechs handling billions of pounds in transactions could lose customers if they lost confidence in their security.

With cyberattacks increasingly linked to geopolitical tensions, Wilson argued that protecting that trust had become a business priority, rather than simply something for the IT department to worry about.

Trust starts with understanding your customers

For Hannah Morrison, founder of Clear Creator, a consultancy that helps financial services businesses put Consumer Duty requirements into practice, trust was more about whether financial products actually work for the people using them.

Speaking about the FCA’s Consumer Duty, she shared her experience of helping her brother become more independent. He’d made huge progress, including getting himself to work on the Tube every day, but managing his finances and benefits was still proving difficult.

“One of the main things he struggles with still is digital products and understanding his finances,” she said.

Morrison said financial products often assume people understand the terminology or know their way around an app, when that isn’t always the case. Even something as basic as terms and conditions can be difficult to understand.

“How do you make those terms and conditions understandable, especially for people who might not necessarily have that background knowledge?” she asked.

For Morrison, getting Consumer Duty right means understanding customers properly, including those with additional needs, and checking whether they’re actually getting a good service. She argued that businesses benefit too, with happier customers, less rework and fewer problems further down the line.

“They trust you again,” she said, before adding with a nod to the day’s discussions: “We’re coming back to this theme of trust.”

Can we trust ourselves to think?

With AI doing more of the work, there was also plenty of discussion about what happens to the people using it.

During a panel on fintech talent and skills, Dr Ashleigh McLellan, co-founder of leadership consultancy Anumi, joined Macs Dickinson, director of engineering at LHV Bank, and Crispin Read, CEO of The Coders Guild, to talk about how AI is changing the skills employers need.

Dickinson said LHV Bank had already changed the way it interviews engineers. Candidates can use AI during assessments, but they’re expected to explain their decisions, talk through the trade-offs and show they understand what they’ve produced.

“Not using AI as a substitute for your own intelligence,” he said, was particularly important, warning that people risk losing skills if they rely too heavily on the technology.

McLellan, who has a background in clinical psychology, brought the discussion back to human curiosity and judgement. She questioned whether people were becoming too willing to accept the answers AI gives them, rather than stopping to consider whether they’re right.

Read made a similar point about education, suggesting that schools often teach children to memorise answers rather than encouraging them to experiment, ask questions and learn from mistakes.

And there was another issue: whether people feel comfortable asking questions at work in the first place.

Dickinson talked about trying to create a ‘psychologically safe environment’ for his engineering teams, where nobody was afraid of looking foolish for asking something.

“Is the enemy of curiosity fear?” he pondered.

It brought the discussion back to trust, this time between employers and their staff. As moderator Rhys Griffiths, relationship manager at FinTech Wales, put it: “You build that trust. You build that curiosity.”

A decade of FinTech North

FinTech North is celebrating its 10th anniversary this year, having started with an event in Leeds back in 2016.

General manager Joe Roche told delegates that the North is now home to around 400 fintech businesses, generating approximately £5billion in annual gross value added. Payments businesses account for roughly half of them, although banking, lending, wealthtech and insurtech are also well represented across the region.

The North’s different cities have their own specialisms, and Roche said the aim was for them to collaborate rather than compete.

Indeed, Chelsea Boothroyd from the University of Leeds talked about the Leeds Financial Innovation Exchange, which is bringing financial services organisations, startups and academics together to tackle specific business problems. That includes helping new technology providers find customers, test their products and deal with the sometimes lengthy process of getting their solutions into large financial institutions.

Then Steve Kevan, CEO and co-founder of FinPact, introduced the Edge AI Skills Programme, developed with Newcastle College Group and MediaWorks, with a pilot involving 25 learners already underway.

The programme covers everything from basic AI literacy to more advanced skills, with a focus on using the technology safely and being able to demonstrate that people know what they’re doing.

Kevan mentioned hearing about one large organisation where 40 people were apparently building the same AI agent, each unaware that others were doing the same thing.

AI was already bringing productivity gains to businesses, he said, but there was still that word again: trust.

“Are we using it properly? Are we using it properly within the organisation or as individuals?” he asked.

fullText:
Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series.

  

Speaker: Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer

Event: Bloomberg UK Policy Series

Delivered: 19 October 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version

Reading time: 8 minutes

Highlights

We want the UK to be at the forefront of the safe and responsible adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in financial services, supporting innovation, productivity and economic growth.

As AI evolves towards increasingly autonomous systems, firms should put consumers first, maintain clear accountability and plan for when things go wrong.

We are sharing examples of good and poor AI practice to help firms innovate responsibly, with a focus on putting consumers first, ensuring clear accountability and planning for failure.

The FCA is becoming a smarter regulator, using AI in its own work and taking forward the Mills Review through engagement, testing and action.

It’s great to be here today with you – humans.

The AI news cycle has become almost impossible to keep up with.

Like many of you, I’m reading a lot – how the race for faster AI chips is driving investment in data centres, creating both growth and risk across equity and debt markets.

Global spend on AI is expected to reach over $2.6 trillion this year.

That same acceleration is playing out across science and technology.

Last week, I visited a Quantum lab to see how AI is advancing cryptographic research.

And I’m fascinated by the way AI builders are turning to neuroscience to analyse the behaviour of agents, following the Hugging Face security incident.

After 25 years working at the intersection of data, technology and innovation, I have never found this field more exciting.

Adoption is not coming. It is here.

ChatGPT has reached over a billion active users.

Across financial services, firms are moving from experimentation to deployment. Our joint AI survey with the Bank of England, published next week, shows 86% of firms now use AI.

AI will redefine financial services. Done well, AI can increase productivity, improve competition, services and drive economic growth.

And the FCA wants the UK to be at the forefront of the safe adoption of AI in financial services.

    

            						

The Mills Review

That is why we commissioned the Mills Review, published in July, focused on how AI could reshape retail financial services by 2030.

Some developments we anticipated are already emerging, including the transition towards agentic finance, such as the launch of Meta’s Muse.

Our response to the review is not to consult, study and report progress. Our focus is testing, assurance, monitoring and surveillance: directly with industry to understand how AI systems are being deployed.

Whilst the Review focused on retail, the AI shift does not stop at the retail boundary. Across wholesale markets too, AI is accelerating how firms analyse, trade, monitor and make decisions.

We are embedding 6 of the 7 recommendations into live work immediately. Our innovation services such as the AI Lab give us direct insight into what firms are building from agent-led payments and fraud detection to consumer support.

On frontier AI security, we are working directly with banks to understand how frontier models are changing cyber defence, identifying and linking vulnerabilities and assisting with triaging, patching and recovering at greater speed. Those insights are feeding directly into our supervisory and policy response.

Firms are not bystanders in that process. The leaders will be those that deploy AI effectively, innovatively and safely.

But increasingly, AI is also changing what happens before a consumer ever reaches a regulated firm. Consumers are turning to general-purpose large language models (LLMs), like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, for financial information and advice, while regulated firms are beginning to integrate their services into AI platforms.

The good news – this can significantly widen access to financial tools and information. But it can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive.

Four in five less-experienced investors aged 18-40 have used AI to help with investing, but only 40% of consumers correctly recognise that there is no recourse if something goes wrong after acting on advice from a general-purpose AI tool. Our answer is not simply to expand our remit, but to make the existing boundary clearer.

Through InvestSmart and the FCA Firm Checker, we already help consumers understand the protections they have. But warnings may be more effective at the point where AI-generated financial information is delivered.

So we are calling on AI providers to help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers.

And rather than create a new public-interest financial capability tool, as the Mills Review suggested, we will build on existing work, including IOSCO’s first TechSprint, powered by our AI Lab to help investors spot scams, verify information and challenge unreliable AI outputs.

          

            						

AI adoption: good and poor practice

Protecting consumers starts with how firms deploy AI.

Today, we are publishing good and poor practice drawn from our observations from firm testing this year, to give practical guidance and examples.

Three things stand out: consumer centricity, accountability and governance, and operational resilience.

Put the consumer first

The Consumer Duty provides an outcomes-based regulatory framework. We’ve seen firms using AI for inclusive product design, clear consumer choice, and a path to speak to a person. Good practice: one firm developed a live list of vulnerability signals that its chatbot can use to flag consumers who may need additional support to human advisers.

But we have seen poor practice too: firms developing AI tools without a clearly defined need, excluding vulnerable consumers by default, overstating capabilities, or deploying automated customer journeys without sufficient testing.

AI should improve consumer outcomes, not simply automate existing processes.

Know who is accountable

The second principle is governance, where too many firms are still under-investing.

Firms need clear accountability, risk-based controls, human oversight, escalation triggers, and senior managers personally accountable for AI systems.

We have seen good examples. One firm established an independent ethics panel to interrogate proposed AI use cases before deployment – including ownership, bias, and controls. But we have also seen firms retrofit governance after technology has already been deployed or fail to adapt monitoring as systems change.

That is the wrong way around.

Operational resilience

Third: stress-test AI systems. Plan for failure. Maintain fallback options. Understand supplier concentrations and dependencies, including reliance on a single model. A system that fails at scale disrupts the services consumers rely on. Make sure you have proper cyber insurance in place.

Overall, our good and poor practice finds that both firms and consumers benefit from well-deployed systems. Even AI deployed purely for internal efficiency passes value to consumers – through better-run firms, more competitive pricing, and faster service.

Our good and poor practice, published today, is not intended to be static guidance – we will update it as the technology evolves.

          

            						

From frontier AI to agentic finance

And the frontier is moving quickly – shifting from technology that helps us understand and decide, to technology that can increasingly act on our behalf.

Agents can search across products, manage payments and investments, and transact directly with other agents, creating a new layer of autonomous technology between institutions and their customers. With its strengths in fintech and financial services, the UK can lead this next wave.

But greater autonomy also changes the risk.

Poorly governed AI can create consumer harm, cyber vulnerabilities and operational failures, potentially at much greater speed and scale.

That is why firms need to invest now in cyber and operational resilience. Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses. As the AI Minister has recognised, near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. It is a regulatory priority too.

It also means thinking differently about assurance. A system that is safe at deployment may behave differently at scale, under stress or as the models beneath it change. Agentic systems therefore require continuous, conditional assurance.

The FCA will work with industry, fellow regulators and frontier labs to develop a trusted framework for agentic finance, including clear approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution.

Our aim is to create the conditions in which agentic finance can thrive, with innovation and consumer protection built together from the start.

          

            						

Becoming an agentic regulator

And the FCA itself is changing. Part of our work to become a smarter regulator means developing our future as an agentic regulator, using the same technologies reshaping our markets to make ourselves sharper, faster, and more effective.

Across the FCA we are deploying AI to scale our operations and focus on the greatest harms, upskilling staff and investing in technology. AI can gather evidence, surface intelligence from disparate sources, and flag early warning signs so we can act at pace.

For example, we are building AI tools for the oversight of 60,000 anti-money laundering (AML) firms coming into the FCA’s remit in 2028. We are deploying automation and building AI agentic tools – like our market first responder agent – which will supervise ~9,000 small wholesale markets transaction reporting firms, so supervisors can prioritise more complex supervisory activities.

Dynamic data collection becomes part of the future of supervision. Building on our launch in August of the FCA’s Handbook API, giving access to firms to digest our machine-readable rules via their AI tools, we are also working on machine-readable data collection APIs.

And leveraging our AI Lab and Sandbox environment becomes ever more important for system-wide simulations and method of supervision.

          

            						

Conclusion

I began by saying it was good to be here among humans. While that was light-hearted, there is a serious point behind the work we must do together.

AI is moving faster than any regulatory framework was designed. That means regulators will increasingly need to make judgements without precedent, while ensuring that trust remains at the heart of financial services.

We remain focused on our strategy, becoming a smarter regulator, using technology to become faster and more effective, enabling markets that work well – for consumers, for growth, and for the long term.

Building on our world-leading approach to innovation and proportionate regulation, we believe developing the best approach to deploying AI safely is what will differentiate the UK market.

The future of finance is being built now. Let's build it together.

title: Butter Payments has been sold
snippet: The company was purchased last month, said its former chief executive, Charles Rosenblatt, who noted intensifying competitive pressures.
fullText:
Butter Payments, a business that has provided services to companies for managing customers’ subscription payments, has been acquired.

The company’s ex-CEO, Charles Rosenblatt, disclosed the sale in an interview last week. “We sold it about three weeks ago,” he said during a Friday interview. On his LinkedIn profile, Rosenblatt said the transaction took place in September.

He declined to name the company that has purchased Butter Payments, but said he expected the acquirer would make an announcement.

Butter Payments' business uses machine-learning algorithms and data from a consumer’s card and payment patterns to better understand why a subscription payment failed and how to resolve the problem. 

“Non-sufficient funds is usually the leading source, but another one of the big ones is suspected fraud,” Rosenblatt said in a February interview.

In a press release earlier this year, Butter Payments cited the churn added up to a collective $440 billion annually in lost revenue for companies with subscription payment methods.

During the interview last week, Rosenblatt explained how the payments business has changed so that services like those offered by Butter Payments have been absorbed into broader suites of services owned by larger companies, causing more competitive pressure from bigger players. It was “very tough as a monoline business,” he said. 

Rosenblatt likened the Butter Payments service to one of the myriad items listed on a restaurant’s menu. “What we built was better than anyone else, but for other companies, we were page 18 of a 20-page Cheesecake Factory menu,” Rosenblatt explained. “We were a better page 18. The problem is, what happens, competitively, is folks come in and offer page 18 for free, if you buy pages one through 17.” 

Digital payments juggernaut Stripe being one of those competitors was part of the problem. Rosenblatt shared how one client told him about the unbeatable offer that Stripe made.

“Stripe basically said to them, all the money they're saving you, we'll just pay you that in cash and take it off your bill to not do business with them and stay with us for everything,” Rosenblatt said. “It's hard to beat that, and that was millions of dollars.”

Facing that kind of competition would have required Butter Payments to raise more funds, so developing an exit plan became the more viable option, the ex-CEO said.

“We had a couple new products, but we … would have had to go raise a ridiculous amount of money to go expand,” Rosenblatt said. “Our investors, candidly, didn't have an appetite for that.”

As of February, the San Francisco-based business had raised nearly $40 million as of earlier this year. At its peak size, Butter Payments had about 53 employees.

Rosenblatt joined Butter Payments in June 2025 as its chief commercial officer, according to his LinkedIn profile. In November of last year, he was promoted to CEO, with marching orders to turn the business around after excessive spending, he said.

Prior to that role, he has been an adviser to investment companies and previously a payments consultant, but he had also held executive posts at companies including PayQuicker, Payoneer and Velo Payments, his LinkedIn profile showed.

Rosenblatt said he has counseled other companies with standalone approaches similar to the Butter Payments business to be aware of the encroaching competition.

“My big message is, I think you're going to have a hard time as a standalone doing this,” Rosenblatt contended.

As for Rosenblatt, he plans to return to the cross-border payments niche where he spent much of his career. He’s on the hunt for new opportunities at the Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas this week.

title: AI’s real opportunity in payments is giving experts back their time
snippet: Advancing operational efficiency through intelligent guidance on errors and exception handling.

Picture a payments operator working through an exception queue. An item kicks out, and before it can be fixed, someone has to determine why: pull the transaction data, trace it through the relevant systems, check it against the rules of the network it is moving through and then decide on a corrective action. That kind of process plays out again and again across a bank's payment operations, every day, many times a day. Payment processing errors and exception handling remain both a heavy manual burden on operations teams and a detractor for overall end-customer experience, with disruptions costing the industry billions of dollars every year.

As payment volumes continue to rise, there is a big opportunity for banks to address this persistent pain point in payment operations and fuel growth. AI-driven automation that maintains human oversight offers a promising way to reimagine inefficient payment error and exception-handling processes by accelerating repairs, streamlining onboarding and improving the overall customer experience.

Accelerating repairs

Now consider that same operator working from a different starting point. AI has already surfaced the likely cause of the discrepancy, checked it against the applicable payment rules and recommended a fix. The operator reviews an assembled case, corrects it where needed and approves it, rather than building it from scratch. That is a faster task. Finastra’s data shows that this kind of guidance can reduce manual investigation time by 20-30%, saving payment operations teams more than 1.5 hours a day that would otherwise be spent diagnosing the same category of problem without this capability. That speed creates real operational capacity, enabling teams to handle more high-value customer experiences and create differentiation.

Enhancing operator onboarding

Payments infrastructure at most financial institutions is complex, built on years of integrations with institutional knowledge often concentrated among a handful of experienced staff. This makes learning a bank's payment systems no small task and places a premium on specialized skillsets. AI-powered automation capabilities targeted to support payment error reconciliation can shorten the learning curve by acting as a guide, helping new hires navigate the system and find the documentation or precedent they need. Just as important, it augments the specialized human expertise within organizations, since reliable repair guidance is now built into the workflow.

Becoming resilient and future proof

Payment rails are not static. Real-time schemes continue to roll out, ISO 20022 migration is reshaping message standards across markets, and cross-border corridors carry their own compliance requirements. A recommendation that is not validated against the current rules of the network a payment is moving through, such as SWIFT, Fedwire, SEPA, UPI or Nexus, cannot be trusted. Scheme-aware repair recommendations should identify discrepancies and underlying causes, delivering a proposed fix that is accurate and compliant with scheme and network requirements. With cloud-native infrastructure, AI-powered payments reconciliation recommender capabilities provide the flexibility to update rules without multi-year re-platforming whenever a standard changes. That combination is what resilience means in payment operations: staying accurate and compliant as the rules governing payments continue to change.

Modernization and AI readiness are becoming less of an efficiency upgrade and more of a growth requirement. The time, manual effort and specialized expertise required to keep error and exception-handling operations running smoothly have, for years, limited how quickly banks can scale. Solving that back-office barrier is part of what will separate the institutions that grow from those that do not.

On 13 October, 3 individuals were arrested following a joint operation by the FCA and the National Crime Agency (NCA). More than 100 FCA and NCA staff took part in searches at 5 residential premises in London and Manchester.

All 3 suspects are in the process of being interviewed by the FCA at police stations in London and Manchester.
