fullText:
Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026.

  

Speaker: Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive

Event: Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026, Guildhall, City of London

Delivered: 20 October 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Reading time: 6 minutes

Highlights

In an ever-changing environment, our strategy is our anchor. Our priorities – supporting growth, being a smarter regulator, helping consumers and fighting financial crime – help us decide consistently and act for the long term.  

While we are past the peak of rule making, we are still taking a deliberate, strategic approach to reform rather than taking a piecemeal approach.

We encourage firms to engage with us. Tell us where the friction lies so we can build a system that works together.

Look around.

This building has stood for more than 600 years. It’s survived both the Great Fire and the Blitz. 

And yet it still endures. Because when it had to be, it was rebuilt deliberately.

That’s the lesson I want to borrow tonight.

The world around Guildhall looks nothing like it did – and neither does your industry. Technology and AI mean markets are changing faster, and more fundamentally, than ever before.

But one thing is constant. 

Markets have always been rooted in trust.

Trust is fundamental to the success of your sector.

And it is a successful sector. 

London ranks second globally in the Global Financial Centres Index, just behind New York.

And millions trust you with their savings. Their pensions. Their very futures.

Total assets under management have now reached £16.5tn – that’s nearly 5 times the UK’s GDP.

But success is no reason to stand still.  

    

            						

Reform: more than writing rules

In this sector, we’re just past peak rule making.  

The scale of change has been significant – and deliberate.

But we’re not done yet.

We want to see growth that benefits consumers, supports competitiveness and spurs innovation.

Building a stronger retail investment culture takes more than piecemeal rule writing.

It takes a strategic approach.  

One that starts with giving consumers the support they need to make informed financial decisions. 

And understand both the risks of acting – and the costs of not acting.

In that vein, we have reformed our advice and guidance rules.

We’ve introduced targeted support.

And we’ve moved away from prescriptive disclosures, and placed greater emphasis on outcomes through the Consumer Duty.

We want to further support innovation and give firms the confidence to offer more forms of simplified advice at lower cost to consumers.

So we’ll soon publish updated rules, alongside case studies we’ve developed with the Financial Ombudsman Service.

We’re already seeing real progress.

Just 6 months in, more than a dozen firms are already authorised to deliver targeted support.

And early signs are promising: consumers who receive it invest up to 53% more than those who don’t.

These reforms have taken time and effort – from your teams, and mine.

But it’s well worth it.

          

            						

Our report card

Last year we set out a new 5-year strategy.

To support growth, be a smarter regulator, help consumers navigate their financial lives and fight financial crime.

These aren’t separate goals. Each one helps us do our job of making markets work well.  

We’re pleased with the progress we’ve made so far.

Our latest Practitioner Panel survey found that three quarters of firms have high trust in us, and the same proportion support our strategy.

More than 7 in 10 agree our work enhances the UK’s reputation as a financial centre.  

And nearly 9 in 10 now understand the Consumer Duty’s requirements – a big change from last year.

But we know there’s more to do. 

Which is why we’ll stay focused on reducing burden, including by simplifying data returns.

And expand our innovation services, where applications rose 89% in the first year of our strategy.

From our Scale-up Unit to our AI sandboxes, we’re helping firms access funding, test new ideas and innovate more quickly.

And we’ll keep sharing what we learn to help firms innovate effectively. 

          

            						

Challenges ahead

Still, financial crime remains a challenge – at home and abroad.

In the UK, investment fraud losses alone rose 40% in 2025.  

And that’s despite us being ever more assertive.

We’re securing more criminal convictions than ever before across fraud, money laundering and insider dealing.

Last year, we issued over 2,300 scam and unauthorised firm warnings.

And in recent weeks, we’ve made 3 arrests as part of a major insider dealing investigation and helped the Metropolitan Police disrupt a suspected serious organised crime network.

But intervention is just part of the equation.

Regulator and industry alike have to help consumers use financial services safely.

The Investment Association has Savvy the Squirrel to help build confidence to invest.

And we have Emil the Seal to point people to our Firm Checker.

Since its launch in January, consumers have used it nearly 2 million times to make sure firms are authorised and genuine.

A partnership between Emil and Savvy could be a powerful one, especially if firms point consumers to Firm Checker. 

What is clear is that with the speed and scale of this threat, we can’t do this on our own.

This fight calls for a system-wide response – because scams undermine trust, market integrity and consumer confidence.

So work with us.

In July, we published our review of financial crime controls in asset management and alternatives.

We found good practice and room for improvement – particularly in higher-risk areas, such as private markets.

Our message is clear: tailor your financial crime controls to the risks.

Our ask is clear, too: share intelligence early. Flag the gaps in the system. And help us stop criminals exploiting them.

It’s how markets stay trusted and confident.

          

            						

Working differently to support a changing world

Change is happening at a breakneck speed.

More technology. More cross-border activity. More innovation.

All moving faster than traditional regulation can keep up with.  

Which is why we’re not just regulating for the market as it is today. We’re future-proofing it.

By setting clear, outcomes-focused standards, using better data to spot emerging risks and keeping our rules under review as markets evolve.  

That approach keeps us open-minded in the face of change. 

And our regulation and rulebook proportionate and fit for the future.  

Take the package of reforms we consulted on this summer. By streamlining the rulebook for asset managers, we could save firms £128m per year.  

Our proposed fund reporting framework is part of that: simpler reporting for firms, better data for us to consider as we review our rules and see how markets are operating.  

We’re collecting responses until Thursday, so there’s still time to have your say. 

I’ve always said we can’t regulate just for yesterday’s challenges. We have to let markets evolve.  

And we are.

We worked previously to support industry and IA-led blueprints for fund tokenisation.  

Now, we’re helping firms put them into practice.

Baillie Gifford tested the technology behind its tokenised fund in our regulatory sandbox. That fund was authorised in under a year.  

Next month, our joint tokenisation roadmap with the Bank of England will set the path from testing to lasting infrastructure for markets as a whole.  

But change also demands preparation.  

With T+1 settlement less than a year away, we are focused on this sector’s readiness.

So be prepared – because we will act if you’re not. 

After all, market integrity is at stake. 

Getting outcomes-focused regulation right means you don’t need to wait for new rules to innovate.

And this will move us beyond a cycle of constant rule making to one of us checking that our rules work as intended.

We already do this regularly.  

You’ve seen it in the removal of rules requiring a 7-day delay in initial public offerings. 

Our review of the Consumer Duty’s application to wholesale markets. 

And our Advice Guidance Boundary Review and unbundling of research rules.

You’ve also just heard me say we’re just past the peak of rule making.

While it may not feel like it yet, it will eventually – I promise!  

When it does, our focus will be clear. 

Keep what works. Fix what doesn’t. And keep growth and innovation at the centre of it.

          

            						

Becoming the regulator of the future

Being the right kind of regulator means being right for today and tomorrow.

Later this week at Mansion House, our chief executive will speak about what a changing world means for modern regulators.

The same question applies here.

There are more opportunities – for firms and criminals – than ever before. And we have to meet them differently. 

By making better use of data and technology and focusing our supervision where risk actually sits.

AI already helps us cut through large data sets to identify risks sooner and act more quickly.

We'll keep exploring where we can go from here. Because we don’t know what tomorrow holds.

But we know we have to be a regulator that moves as fast as the market does, without losing the judgement that makes us worth trusting.

And you have to be an industry that’s just as intentional. One that moves quickly where it counts, without losing sight of the people who depend on you.

          

            						

A shared responsibility

We all want a more predictable, proportionate and purposeful regulatory system.

We’ll only get there by being deliberate, with the future in mind – as this building reminds us.

So, keep telling us where the tension is, and continue engaging with the reforms already underway.

The prize is worth it: a regulatory framework that supports growth and encourages investment while protecting consumers and earning trust.

Not just for today – but for tomorrow.

title: Money20/20 USA day two: the risk question moves into the plumbing
snippet: Day one asked who carries the risk when money moves itself. Day two showed the industry building the answer into standards and code, not waiting for regulators. The post Money20/20 USA day two: the risk question moves into the plumbing appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Day one asked who carries the risk when money moves itself. Day two showed the industry building the answer into standards and code, not waiting for regulators.

Day one at Money20/20 USA kept circling one question: when money moves itself, who carries the risk? On Tuesday the question did not go away, but it changed shape. Across the stages and in the news coming off the floor, the industry stopped waiting for someone else to answer it and started building the answer into standards, certificates and code. And the contest between tokenised deposits and stablecoins, still live on Monday, came close to being called off.

From who pays to who vouches

On Monday the liability question was asked about agents: if an AI buys something its owner did not intend, the issuer needs to know which agent it was and what it was allowed to do. On Tuesday the same logic was applied to everyone in the chain. In his keynote conversation with Penny Lee of the Financial Technology Association, The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) Chairman Travis Hill described the standard-setting body the agency has been helping banks and fintechs design since the summer. Instead of every community bank running its own due diligence on the same fintech, independent assessors would check third parties against common standards that small banks can rely on. It would be run by the industry, and “this would be completely voluntary”.

The same idea is spreading to agents. Visa, BILL and Billtrust announced the first live pilot in which an AI agent pays supplier invoices through supplier portals, registered through Visa’s Trusted Agent Protocol and recognised by the supplier’s platform in place of the login and CAPTCHA a person would face. Evervault launched short-lived tokens that let an agent complete a checkout without ever holding card numbers or passwords, pitched as an alternative to the networks’ own agent programmes. Elliptic launched a free certification for the compliance staff who will have to supervise agents, alongside research in which only 16 per cent of 318 senior risk and compliance professionals were very confident their team could govern an AI agent today.

What has not changed is who answers in the end. Asked who carries the liability as identity data passes between firms, Hill said the deeper questions sit outside the FDIC’s remit and described fraud as a whole-of-government effort. On Monday former CFTC Chairman Chris Giancarlo argued for letting innovation run ahead of the rules. On liability, at least, Tuesday showed it already has.

The controls are now the bottleneck

The show’s own theme is speed, and Lee put the obvious follow-up to Hill: if payments are getting faster, so is fraud. He said new AI tools make identity harder at both ends, when an account is opened and every time it is used, and that the FDIC is working with the Treasury on a longer-term approach. The most practical point was about money that should not leave. Rules require banks to release funds quickly, but where fraud is obvious it may be in everyone’s interest for the bank to hold them, and Hill said there have been discussions with the Federal Reserve about those rules.

The rails are speeding up regardless. Nacha reported 470.4 million Same Day ACH payments in the third quarter, up 36.7 per cent on a year earlier, on the same day the show was debating agents that pay around the clock. Monday’s message was that trust has to be built before scale. Tuesday’s was that the controls built for a slower system, from identity checks at account opening to the rules on releasing funds, are now what holds scale back.

Deposits and stablecoins stop competing

On Monday Will Artingstall, Citi’s head of banking as a service, said the bank had seen strong take-up of tokenised deposits, because clients never have to hold a wallet. On Tuesday, on the panel on tokenised assets and stablecoins, the bank went further: it offers both, partners with Coinbase on stablecoins and is part of a consortium looking at issuing one. “I think it’s an and,” said Ryan Rugg, its global head of digital assets for treasury and trade.

The stablecoin side met the banks halfway. Stripe and Coinbase are both founders of Open USD, the shared stablecoin announced in June that is designed to pass reserve revenue back to the businesses that use it. Shan Aggarwal, Coinbase’s chief business officer, argued that the blocker is no longer technology but coordination: custodians, clearing houses and banks still have to treat a stablecoin as a full dollar, and a clearing house that credits 90 cents for one gives customers every reason not to use it. Neetika Bansal of Stripe said customers rarely ask for stablecoins any more; they ask for cross-border payments that arrive.

That picks up Monday’s theme of the invisible rail. Rugg expects blockchain to go the way of cloud, something nobody asks about, and Aggarwal hopes the category disappears by 2030: “I think we just talk about assets.” The day’s other news pointed the same way: TD Bank said third-party apps will move onto secure API connections through Akoya from the fourth quarter, and Cross River, one of the best-known banks behind fintech products, agreed to buy the branded wallet business Accrue.

What the next conversations will be

Three questions came out of Tuesday that will run well beyond Las Vegas. The first is who vouches for an agent. The FDIC’s voluntary standards body is designed for fintech partners, but its model of common standards and independent assessors is exactly what the agent pilots are reaching for, and the confidence gap Elliptic measured suggests compliance teams know it.

The second is how regulators treat the two forms of digital money now that the market has decided it wants both. The OCC’s final rule under the GENIUS Act is expected before the end of October, and a week before the show Hill said the FDIC will have more work to do on tokenised deposits afterwards, including how to resolve a failed bank whose deposits move at weekends.

The third is the plumbing that turns all of this into ordinary money: clearing houses that accept a stablecoin at face value, banks allowed to hold suspect funds, and payments small enough for agents to make by the thousand. Bansal called stablecoins “agent native money”. Day two suggested the industry agrees. It has not yet agreed who is accountable when that money goes wrong.

Victims of a £1.5m crypto investment fraud will recover lost funds after the FCA obtained confiscation orders against Raymondip Bedi and Patrick Mavanga.

  

            						

At a hearing at Southwark Crown Court on 28 September 2026, Raymondip Bedi was ordered to pay £603,404.28 and Patrick Mavanga £247,997.99.

Between February 2017 and June 2019, Bedi and Mavanga operated a fraudulent investment scheme, cold-calling consumers and persuading them to invest in fake cryptoasset opportunities through companies including CCX Capital and Astaria Group LLP. At least 65 investors were defrauded and lost £1,541,799.

The FCA has identified and contacted victims of the fraud and will ensure that funds recovered through the confiscation process are returned to victims.

In July 2025, following an FCA prosecution, Raymondip Bedi was sentenced to 5 years and 4 months' imprisonment and Patrick Mavanga was sentenced to 6 years and 6 months' imprisonment for their roles in the scheme.

Steve Smart, joint executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:

'Bedi and Mavanga defrauded investors and left them out of pocket. These orders bring victims a step closer to getting money back.

'We’ll keep coming after fraudsters and holding them to account.'

Notes to editors

Raymondip Bedi’s date of birth is 9 October 1989.

title: 46% of UK Mortgages at High Income Multiples as Long-Term Risk Grows
snippet: Sprive CEO Jinesh Vohra warns the mortgage industry is failing borrowers on lifetime cost as high loan-to-income lending rises sharply. The post 46% of UK Mortgages at High Income Multiples as Long-Term Risk Grows appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Nearly half of all gross mortgage advances in the UK during the second quarter of 2026 were made to borrowers at high loan-to-income ratios, according to figures from the FCA and Bank of England. That share rose to 46% from 41.4% a year earlier, a trajectory that Jinesh Vohra, chief executive and co-founder of mortgage overpayment platform Sprive, says signals a structural problem the industry is not adequately addressing.

Jinesh Vohra, CEO and founder at Sprive

Vohra made the remarks on the latest episode of Twenty7tec‘s ELEVATE Podcast Series, in conversation with host Ellisha Jade. His central argument is that monthly affordability has become the dominant frame for mortgage decisions, while the lifetime cost of debt receives far less attention from lenders, brokers and borrowers alike.

“I think it’s very important that people understand the cost of debt, because it’s not just about meeting the monthly payments,” Vohra said. “You have to be able to do that over the entire lifetime of the mortgage.”

The structural shift in borrowing behaviour

The affordability squeeze has pushed a growing proportion of first-time buyers toward extended mortgage terms of 30 or 40 years. A longer term reduces the monthly payment and brings more borrowers within a lender’s affordability calculation, but it substantially increases the total interest paid and leaves borrowers carrying material debt later into their working lives and, in some cases, into retirement. Research from Yorkshire Building Society cited in the release found that 56% of prospective first-time buyers still consider mortgage acceptance difficult, which suggests the underlying affordability constraint has not eased despite the structural workarounds now in common use.

Compounding this is the pattern of intermittent customer engagement that characterises much of the adviser market. Twenty7tec’s own August 2026 Mortgage Market Snapshot recorded 616,150 remortgage searches, an increase of 11% year on year. That activity reflects borrowers actively reviewing their arrangements, but Vohra argued that two-to-five-year remortgage cycles are not sufficient to provide the ongoing financial support homeowners need.

“If you are interacting with that customer every two to five years, when they’re effectively looking to refinance, how strong is that relationship?” he said.

Regulatory and market context

The rising share of high loan-to-income lending is not new to regulators. The Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee has maintained a flow limit on high loan-to-income mortgage lending since 2014, capping at 15% the proportion of new lending at or above 4.5 times income for any given lender. The Q2 2026 data point of 46% refers to the broader high loan-to-income bracket, not solely those at or above 4.5 times, but the directional trend has attracted regulatory attention as affordability pressure intensifies. Any significant deterioration in borrower resilience at extended terms could prompt the FCA or PRA to revisit the adequacy of affordability stress tests.

Sprive’s own position is that technology and data can support more continuous borrower engagement outside of transaction moments. The platform allows homeowners to direct spending rewards toward mortgage overpayments and provides modelling tools on the impact of early repayment. Vohra’s Series A, a $10 million round announced in September 2026 and bringing total funding to more than $15 million, is earmarked for customer acquisition and revenue growth in the UK market. The commercial thesis rests on sustained customer relationships rather than point-in-time origination, which aligns the product with the structural critique Vohra is making of the wider industry.

For mortgage technology providers and lenders, the debate points to a growing commercial opportunity in post-origination engagement tools, an area where the industry’s existing technology stack, built largely around sourcing and application processing, remains relatively thin.

The FCA and Practitioner Panel annual survey of regulated firms provides valuable insights into how firms think we’re performing.

The latest survey shows 79% of firms are highly satisfied with their relationship with the FCA, up from 74% last year. The proportion of firms rating the FCA as a highly effective regulator also increased from 69% to 76%, while 75% reported high levels of trust.

Firms were most confident in our work to protect consumers (87%), ensure markets work well (85%) and enhance the integrity of the UK financial system (85%). There was a 27-percentage point increase in firms’ understanding of the Secondary International Competitiveness and Growth Objective and a 25-percentage point increase in confidence in our delivery of it.

We took on board feedback from last year’s survey and provided further guidance to help firms embed the Consumer Duty. This year, 88% of firms say they understand what we expect on supporting consumers and embedding the Duty.

The findings also provide valuable insight into where firms would like to see further progress, including on regulatory burden. We’re already simplifying reporting by removing outdated or duplicated data returns for 90% of firms.

Nikhil Rathi, chief executive of the FCA, said: 'A year into our strategy it's encouraging to see growing confidence across many areas of our work. We know there is more to do. For example, while we can’t do our job without the data firms provide, we should continue to simplify requests and make them easier to manage.'

Matt Hammerstein, chair of the FCA Practitioner Panel, said: 'This year’s survey results indicate firms continue to have broadly positive views of the FCA, including strong understanding of expectations under the Consumer Duty and significant growth in confidence in the FCA’s ability to deliver on its secondary objectives focused on growth and competitiveness.

'The Panel is encouraging the FCA to be clearer about the outcomes it expects its priorities to produce, and more vocal about the progress it is making against these, to strengthen confidence in the UK as a leading global financial centre and attractive place to invest.'

In the first year of our strategy, we've delivered an estimated £5.6bn in benefits to consumers and the economy, including launching My FCA, reducing reporting burdens to save firms around £16m annually, and introducing nearly 50 pro-growth measures to boost UK competitiveness and innovation. 

Since the survey was conducted, we’ve continued our work to deliver landmark reforms, including working with HM Treasury and the Financial Ombudsman Service to modernise the redress framework, support industry delivery of the Advice Guidance Boundary Review, regulating Buy Now Pay Later products, establishing a new regime for cryptoassets, and progressing the PISCES private markets framework.

fullText:
Speech by Jon Relleen, director of infrastructure and exchanges, at the Reform of the UK Public and Private Capital Markets Summit 2026.

  

Speaker: Jon Relleen, director of infrastructure and exchanges 

Event: Reform of the UK Public and Private Capital Markets Summit 2026

Delivered: 5 October 2026  

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version

Reading time: 9 minutes

Highlights:

The FCA’s wide-ranging reforms over recent years are making UK capital markets more effective, competitive and attractive.

Trust, market integrity and high standards set the foundations for sustainable growth, and it is crucial that we also enable informed risk-taking.

We’re preparing for tomorrow’s markets by supporting innovation, including tokenisation.

    

            						

The Economic Secretary to the Treasury has discussed the contribution of UK markets to economic growth. 

I want to build on that by talking about the FCA’s role in reforming capital market rules.

The headline is that we've been very busy over the past few years. 

We’ve now completed major aspects of a multi-year programme of work, to ensure capital markets work well for our economy and support growth.

This has already delivered positive changes. But there’s plenty more to come.

We are working on further reforms, while also adapting to rapid changes in markets and use of technology.

In fact, areas such as tokenisation, AI and markets for trading private company shares have become central to our capital markets policy programme. 

And that tells us something important. As markets change, our approach has had to change too.

The question has not been whether regulation changes. It has been how we adjust in a way that preserves trust while also supporting innovation and growth.

Let me start by talking about our approach to the work.

We have been working with the Treasury, the Bank of England and in close dialogue with the private sector, on a raft of wholesale market reforms.

These draw on formal reports, like the Wholesale Markets Review, our process of reviewing inherited EU regulation, and issues raised by market contacts.

Some have suggested the work programme is a list not a strategy. But I think that underestimates it. There are some key principles running through it.

          

            						

Reforming from a position of strength

First, we are reforming from a position of strength, by building on the UK’s advantages.

The UK is home to deep, trusted and internationally connected capital markets. 

London continues to rank among the world’s leading financial centres. Our markets are respected and characterised by strong institutions and a reputation for integrity.

And the UK offers a full range of markets and services, supported by a diverse system of issuers, investors, intermediaries and infrastructure.

So our work programme is broad too. Covering primary markets, secondary markets, post-trade arrangements and a broad range of assets.

But successful markets cannot stand still.

Capital is increasingly mobile. Technology is reshaping markets. Private markets have grown. And new forms of trading and market infrastructure are emerging.

So our challenge is to preserve these strengths, whilst keeping UK markets dynamic and internationally competitive.

          

            						

Rebalancing risk

In some areas this requires us to think differently about regulation.

For a while, financial regulation became more detailed and prescriptive. Often for understandable reasons following periods of market stress.

But we know that growth, innovation and investment all depend on taking risk.

That is why our approach is founded on the principle of maintaining high standards while creating more space for informed risk-taking and innovation. 

This is especially relevant in wholesale markets, where professional participants assess opportunities and weigh risks every day.

Our role is to create regulation that enables this through clear rules and good disclosures, so that firms and investors can make informed decisions.

This is what we mean when we talk about rebalancing risk.

It does not mean lowering standards or weakening market integrity.

It means being deliberate about where regulation is needed and where market participants can take decisions themselves, armed with good information and appropriate disclosures.

In many cases, that means we can shift away from detailed prescription towards outcomes, transparency and accountability.

In doing so, we must never forget the underlying objective.

Ultimately, we want companies to have good options for how to raise capital, so they can invest and grow. And investors to have access to a broad range of investment opportunities.

Regulation cannot, on its own, drive economic growth. But good regulation and markets that work well are vital for a healthy economy.

          

            						

Turning reform into results

You can see our approach in the reforms we have already delivered.

We have completed around 30 capital-markets focused workstreams. And there’s an even larger number across the FCA’s broader work.

That’s too many to discuss individually in this speech. There’s a list below, but to summarise some of them:

In primary markets, we introduced once-in-a-generation changes to the UK listing regime, significantly reducing costs for issuers and supporting competitiveness with other jurisdictions. Since then, we have seen many corporate transactions that have been simplified as a result. And around 25 companies have joined the Main Market, including 7 IPOs in H1 2026.

Our new public offers framework raised the thresholds for when prospectuses are needed by companies raising capital and we also introduced public offer platforms to facilitate off-market fundraising. We have already seen a rise in capital raised by companies, including via debt markets, alongside the broader benefits of a simpler and more flexible regime.

In secondary markets, we have significantly improved transparency in bond and derivatives markets. This includes the bond consolidated tape, which launched in June – the first consolidated tape outside North America – which already has 1.6 million licences subscribed to it. These changes are shining a new light on UK markets, delivering a 70% increase in corporate bond trades and 30% for government bond trades observed in real time and enhancing the way market participants view the market.

We are moving towards an equity consolidated tape too and will appoint a provider next year. In the meantime, we launched a market activity report, so investors see the true scale of UK equity trading.

We have also responded to the growth of private markets through the creation of PISCES, a new market for trading in private company shares. Four operators have been authorised and we’ve seen seven transactions – involving companies ranging from tech firms, to brewers and board-game makers.

In post-trade, we’ve adjusted transaction reporting, with initial proposals estimated to save firms £100m per year.

And we’ve altered some of the clearing and margining rules, including increasing the clearing threshold for commodity derivatives following volatility in commodity markets.

On the investor side, we are streamlining regulatory requirements for the asset management sector, via the AIFMD review, and supporting the government in its review of the pension market.

We’re also supporting retail participation by improving access to investment advice and simplifying product information.

And our changes to primary market rules have positively impacted retail investment. We’ve seen a 50% increase in the value of retail-denominated corporate bonds and an increase in domestic retail investor allocation in fundraisings.

We are not done though.

A range of further reforms are planned or underway.

For example, on securitisation markets; listed company disclosures; benchmarks; and rules on clearing and margining.

We’re always in listening mode. So if you have ideas that would benefit UK markets please tell us.

          

            						

Competitiveness without compromise

We are doing this work to make markets work better, which is our statutory objective.

By doing that, we support growth and international competitiveness.

Capital is mobile. Businesses have choices about where they raise finance, invest and operate. The UK cannot ignore that reality.

But competitiveness does not come from a race to the bottom.

The UK's reputation for openness, stability and high standards is a strategic asset.

Our approach is pragmatic. We will challenge inherited rules when they no longer serve markets effectively, learn from other jurisdictions, and recognise the value of international consistency.

But we will do so without compromising market integrity, which provides the bedrock for sustainable growth.

          

            						

Preparing for tomorrow’s markets

I want to finish by talking about how we’re preparing for tomorrow’s markets.

We want to support innovation. To ensure markets evolve and use technology that opens up opportunities, efficiencies and encourages new entrants.

One example is working with firms to support the safe and responsible adoption of AI. Through our AI Lab, the AI Consortium with the Bank, and innovation sandboxes that allow firms to test ideas with us. 

And we are enabling firms and markets to explore tokenisation.

With the Bank and Treasury, we set up the Digital Securities Sandbox, which will support issuance of the new digital gilt (or DIGIT) early next year. Many think that the success of DIGIT can catalyse digital activity in UK.

We have worked with industry on new rules and governance for tokenised investment funds and the launch of the UK’s first fully-native tokenised fund.

And with Treasury and the Bank we’ve developed a regulatory framework for stablecoins.

But we are at a critical point. Keeping pace with other jurisdictions will require effective coordination between the private and public sectors. Industry leadership will be at least as important as public policy. 

Firms need to build, scale and innovate, moving beyond pilots to demonstrate real commercial use.

The UK’s Wholesale Digital Markets Champion, Chris Woolard, is playing a key role in coordinating the sector.

We know that regulatory clarity matters too. That’s why in May we published a joint vision with the Bank of England, setting out the regulatory principles for tokenised wholesale markets.

The feedback was clear. Industry wants to move quickly. In turn, we will provide certainty in areas such as prudential treatment, custody and market infrastructure.

We share the sense of urgency.

In coming weeks we will publish a joint roadmap, setting out how the UK’s wholesale markets will adapt as we work collectively to realise the benefits from tokenisation and digitalization.

Our objective is not to predict exactly what future markets will look like.

It is to ensure that our regulatory framework can adapt as markets evolve.

          

            						

Conclusion

We want UK capital markets to remain among the most trusted in the world, whilst also being among the most innovative, competitive and attractive. Markets that allow businesses to raise capital, help investors, and support the wider economy.

Our wide-ranging reforms have already delivered positive outcomes, across a variety of markets.

The approach is to build on the UK’s strengths and enable informed risk-taking, while preserving the trust, integrity and high standards on which successful markets depend.

The programme of reform will continue to evolve as markets change.

But the direction is clear. We are building markets that are ready not only for today's economy but for tomorrow's as well.

          

        

Capital market reforms completed in recent years

    

      

      						Primary markets
			
    

    

						

Once in a generation reforms to UK equity listing rules.

Read PS24/6: Primary Markets Effectiveness Review: Feedback to CP23/31 and final UK Listing Rules

 A new public offers and admissions to trading regime, making it easier for companies to raise capital, including for further capital raisings and encouraging issuance of low-denomination bonds.

Read PS25/9: New rules for the public offers and admissions to trading regime

Creating rules for public offer platforms, a new regime for 'off-market' capital raisings.

Read PS25/10: Final rules for public offer platforms

Adjusting the rules around unconnected research to speed up the IPO timeline by 7 days.

Read PS26/16: Changes to information flows for UK equity IPOs

The initial stage of reforms to UK securitisation markets.

Read PS24/4: Rules relating to Securitisation

 Aligning listed issuers’ sustainability disclosures with international standards.

Read PS26/19: Aligning listed issuers' sustainability disclosures with international standards

			

  

      

      						Post-trade, investors and cross-cutting
			
    

    

						

Adjustments to the transaction reporting regime under UK MiFIR.

Read PS26/15: Improving the UK transaction reporting regime

With the PRA, making permanent the exemption for single stock equity options and index options from bilateral margining requirements.

Read PRA PS18/23: Margin requirements for non-centrally cleared derivatives: Amendments to BTS 2016/2251

title: Utah forms digital ID consortium
snippet: The state is using its digital identity law as a model for having individuals, not governments, control their personal data, Utah’s chief privacy officer said.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

The state is using its digital identity law as a model for having individuals, not governments, control their personal data, Utah’s chief privacy officer said.

        

            

        Published Oct. 19, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                States are working together to craft regulations related to digital identities. It's an important issue in payments because personal data is tied to transactions.
            
        
            Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Utah is forming a multi-state consortium of governors to advance a governance framework and principles for state-issued digital identification credentials, Utah’s chief privacy officer said Sunday on the first day of the Money20/20 financial technology conference. The coalition is focused on advancing the idea that people inherently own their identification data and should be able to limit how much personal information they share through their digital IDs.

Utah hasn’t announced which states have joined the group, and is awaiting “a few more that will be aligning around these shared principles,” Christopher Bramwell, Utah’s chief privacy officer, said at the discussion on digital identification. By January, 10 states will have either their legislatures or executive branches working on ID governance frameworks modeled after Utah’s privacy-focused “state-endorsed digital identity" program, he said.

States such as Utah and California have been leading in the area of digital identity, said Jennifer Kerber, head of global government affairs for Socure, a digital ID verification and fraud-prevention firm, who spoke with Bramwell during the Sunday panel. California has about 2.2 million digital IDs in use, she said.

Dive Insight:

Digital identities raise important issues in the payments realm because such personal information is often tied to transactions, particularly in e-commerce. That's becoming an increasingly key issue as more fintechs aim to use that data to personalize services.

Currently, 21 states and Puerto Rico issue digital IDs, according to the Transportation Security Administration. 

Utah enacted what it called the first digital ID “bill of rights” law earlier this year, which created a “state-endorsed digital identity” program aimed at giving people control of their identity data.

“What good is digital identity if nothing in it says that somebody can't use it to do surveillance pricing in a way that harms you, or they can't track and surveil every single usage of it?” said Bramwell, who is also director of the Utah Office of Data Privacy.

States need a governance framework for IDs because there are “168 million different digital identities in use across different platforms in the U.S. lacking these rules of the road,” he said.

Ajay Gupta, chief digital transformation officer for the California Department of Motor Vehicles, was also scheduled to appear at the panel. Ultimately, he didn’t appear, with Kerber pointing to travel complications.

Utah is working toward an ID system that would render a person’s data, if it’s breached, virtually useless for fraud and impersonation, because the criminal doesn’t have access to the ID credentials, he said. “How do we empower each of you to have something you control, so that even when your personal data has been breached, it can't be used to impersonate you and commit fraud?” he said. 

Utah began its digital ID work by establishing a policy framework before issuing any products, Bramwell said. With the policy framework passed, Utah officials have begun working on the technology to power the new IDs. “Now we're working on the tech to actually come in and say, ‘What are we actually able to do?’” Bramwell said.

The range of digital IDs across states so far has provided Utah insights on various approaches, he said. 

Utah hopes that as it works with other states, “we actually end up meeting in the middle where we bring the governance, they brought some of the tech, and we'll all be able to exist in this ecosystem, regardless of which technology approach,” Bramwell said.

title: Carta Wins Luxembourg PSF Licence to Unify Fund Administration
snippet: Carta has secured CSSF authorisation as a Specialised Professional of the Financial Sector, adding licensed fund administration and transfer agency in Luxembourg. The post Carta Wins Luxembourg PSF Licence to Unify Fund Administration appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Carta, the private capital platform, has received authorisation as a fully licensed Specialised Professional of the Financial Sector (PSF) from Luxembourg’s financial regulator, the Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier (CSSF). The licence covers five statutory functions: registrar agent, corporate domiciliation agent, company incorporation and management services, administrative agent of the financial sector, and client communication agent.

The authorisation means Carta can now offer licensed fund administration and transfer agency services directly within its platform for Luxembourg-domiciled fund structures, completing what the company describes as the final gap in its Luxembourg proposition. Existing clients running parallel or feeder funds through Luxembourg can now consolidate onto a single system of record across jurisdictions, replacing the fragmented arrangements that have long been a friction point in cross-border fund administration.

Why Luxembourg matters

Yves Cheret, managing director at Carta Luxembourg

Luxembourg is the second-largest fund domicile in the world, home to around 5,000 alternative investment fund entities managing in excess of €1 trillion in assets. The jurisdiction also serves as the preferred hub for more than 1,000 US and Asia-Pacific fund managers running parallel or feeder structures, with those vehicles representing more than $333 billion in assets under management. That combination of scale and structural complexity makes fund administration there operationally demanding: managers have historically had to maintain separate systems and counterparty relationships for each function and jurisdiction, with manual reconciliation to bridge the gaps.

Yves Cheret, authorised manager at Carta, framed the authorisation in operational rather than marketing terms. “Parallel funds, feeder structures, multi-jurisdictional reporting, complex KYC flows: this is exactly the environment where having everything on one connected system of record makes the difference,” he said.

Alongside the licence, Carta has made several platform capabilities live. Lux Closings supports compliant closings across RAIF, SIF and SICAR structures and applicable entity types. A unified KYC form with real-time status tracking gives general partners visibility into limited partner onboarding inside the same system. The company says 90% of cash transactions auto-reconcile within 24 hours and 90% of capital calls are set up within 24 hours, with AI-assisted workflows subject to human verification in line with CSSF requirements.

Competitive and regulatory context

Carta’s move into licensed Luxembourg fund administration places it in direct competition with specialist administrators, many of which have operated under PSF licences for decades and maintain deep depositary bank relationships. The company has framed its differentiation around platform consolidation: the argument that a single system for fund accounting, KYC, closings, LP portfolio analytics and loan operations reduces reconciliation cost and data error, rather than competing on price or local relationship networks.

Four acquisitions over the past year, covering LP Portfolio Analytics, Loan Operations, Carta CRM and Carta Law, have extended the platform into what Carta positions as a full enterprise resource planning suite for private markets. That breadth carries a regulatory overhead: each function within a PSF licence sits under its own CSSF supervisory expectation, and expanding the product footprint within the licence will require ongoing compliance governance.

The regulatory backdrop is also relevant beyond Luxembourg. The EU’s Alternative Investment Fund Managers Directive and its forthcoming revision continue to shape the compliance obligations of administrators servicing European fund structures. Managers using a single-platform administrator will want assurance that the provider can keep pace with regulatory change across jurisdictions simultaneously, rather than prioritising product development at the expense of compliance depth.

Carta says it serves 10,000 funds and SPVs representing $250 billion in assets under management globally. The Luxembourg PSF authorisation is assigned authorisation number 10199274/0.

title: Fiserv taps AI for retail rethink
snippet: Merchants are grappling with how their payments technology will handle artificial intelligence-fueled digital e-commerce, a Fiserv executive said.
fullText:
Agentic commerce is forcing digital merchants to assess whether their technology infrastructure is suited to the coming era of shopping agents powered by artificial intelligence, a Fiserv executive said Tuesday. 

Payments involving AI agents introduce new variables into legacy systems that sellers are now considering, Adit Gadgil, Fiserv’s head of global e-commerce and technology for merchant services, said in an interview at a financial technology conference.

“People are trying to fundamentally evaluate: will their legacy payment stack or commerce stack be fit for purpose, or do they need to build a separate, standalone payment stack to solve the needs of the future, which includes stablecoins, which includes agentic traffic?” Gadgil said.

He spoke a day after Fiserv CEO Tsakis Georgakopoulos told an audience Monday at the conference that AI represents “a general-purpose technology because it impacts every part of the value chain and every industry and every business.”

“It is pretty unique compared to everything else we've seen, at least in our lives,” the CEO added during a Monday panel discussion at the Money20/20 financial technology conference with Rodrigo Kede Lima, president of Microsoft Frontier, the software giant’s AI transformation business. “That creates both problems and opportunities for every industry and every customer segment.”

Earlier this year, Milwaukee-based Fiserv announced “a strategic collaboration” with Microsoft to embed AI solutions into Fiserv’s platforms. Fiserv also uses Microsoft’s AI tools for productivity gains among employees.

Consumers have taken to AI chat tools for product discovery, Georgakopoulos noted, “but the complexity is the last mile.”

“Discovery is great,” he said. “How do you actually click that last button, the checkout button, and will that ever become agentic?”

Gadgil said that, as part of the transition to agentic commerce, merchants will also need to accommodate new “machine readable” digital markets where agents will interact with each other – a change that could render some parts of current systems irrelevant.

“Whether we'll be in this situation, where the (online) surface matters so much, is debatable,” Gadgil said. “That doesn't mean it’s going to disappear, but maybe a percentage of it is going to become irrelevant.”

He added that these new “surfaces” will become “a marketplace for agents to work with each other. If you do not have your market agents showing up at these marketplaces, you may not have the opportunity to do business,” Gadgil said.

Agentic payments may drive between $3 trillion and $5 trillion in global consumer commerce by 2030, according to the consulting firm McKinsey.  

In terms of current technology addressing agentic traffic, online sellers haven’t yet experienced a fundamental change in how their businesses operate because most agentic commerce still involves humans permitting transactions after the agent finds products.

“My opinion on this is that agentic today is essentially another channel,” Gadgil said. “From a payment stack perspective, as long as there's a human in the loop on the authorization, actually you don't really need to change that much” after ensuring where the traffic is from and that no fraud is involved.

Larger changes lie farther in the future, when agents begin transacting autonomously, under rules specified by humans.

This shift will involve adding extra steps within the payments flow, to generate at least two receipts to verify an agent’s actions, he said. The first will be at the intent layer, to prove someone authorized the agent to undertake a specific transaction, with the second detailing all the information about the payment.

Fiserv is working to ensure its merchant clients understand these different aspects of verifying consumer intent and the payment level within agentic commerce, Gadgil said.

“They should be careful with the risk they're taking, and it's not just on the merchant side,” he said, noting that issuers, acquirers and card networks will also require detailed data about agentic transactions. 

“Whether it’s the network or the issuer, they’re all going to be asking these questions, asking for more information, because at the end of the day, no one wants to be sitting there with the liability that comes with it,” Gadgil said.

title: Visa changes fees in Canada
snippet: A Canadian trade group has urged card networks to reduce their interchange fees and pass those cost savings on to sellers.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

A Canadian trade group has urged card networks to reduce their interchange fees and pass those cost savings on to sellers.

        

            

        Published Oct. 21, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                Canadian and American flags fly at the Lewiston-Queenston border crossing bridge. San Francisco-based Visa is shifting gears on card fees for merchants in the neighboring country.
            
        
            Joe Raedle via Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Starting Oct. 24, Canadian small businesses will pay lower interchange fees to accept Visa credit card payments, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business said in a press release on Wednesday. Visa is cutting interchange fees for companies generating up to CA$750,000 ($534,000) in annual Visa sales, according to the release. 

Nonetheless, the card network giant also plans to increase other fees charged to processors that are typically passed onto merchants, adding a 1.8 cent increase to all domestic transactions in Canada, starting next April, the federation said in the release.

“This is a big win for many small businesses that will now qualify for Visa's special, lower interchange rate,” CFIB President Dan Kelly said in the release. “Sadly, there are new credit card processing fees on the horizon as well.”

Dive Insight:

Back in 2024, San Francisco-based Visa and Purchase, New York-based Mastercard entered into an agreement with the Canadian government agency to reduce interchange fees for small businesses. The reduced interchange rates, under that pact, was for businesses with sales below CA$300,000 when it came to Visa’s fees, and for those with sales below CA$175,000 with respect to Mastercard fees. 

While Visa expanded the program to decrease the interchange fee for more small merchants this month, Mastercard is not changing its program parameters under the pact, per the release. The federation pressed Mastercard to follow its larger rival in expanding the program.

"For two decades, CFIB has been pushing for fairer credit card fees for small businesses,” CFIB executive vice president for advocacy, Corinne Pohlmann, said in the release. “We're glad to see Visa include more small merchants, and we are calling on Mastercard and other card brands to do the same."

Visa confirmed the changes, and a spokesperson said the company aims to provide an average interchange rate of 95 basis points for eligible Canadian small merchants on domestic consumer credit card transactions where a customer is present for the purchase.

“This change will enable more Canadian small businesses to benefit from reduced acceptance costs, reinforcing Visa's commitment to supporting small businesses and expanding digital payments acceptance and strengthening the broader Canadian economy,” the Visa spokesperson said by email.

Mastercard didn’t immediately comment on the changes.

The Canadian Federation of Independent Business, which represents small businesses, has been pushing the government and payment providers to require more credit card providers to participate in its rate-reduction initiative, reassess size limits and secure savings for sellers. 

With respect to the added processor fees, Mastercard started charging the new fee to card processors last week, and Visa will do the same beginning in April 2027, the release said.

title: The 67% signal: Why card issuers should act on flexible credentials
snippet: 67% want one card for debit, credit and BNPL. Don’t let a competitor give it to them first.
fullText:
Marqeta’s 2026 State of Credit Report found that 67% of consumers would replace their primary debit card with a flexible credential. This isn’t curiosity but preference, and the gap between what consumers want and what most card programs offer is widening fast.

What’s a flexible credential?

A single payment card that adapts to context. At checkout, the cardholder can pay with debit, draw on a credit line, split the purchase into BNPL installments, or combine funding sources. The form factor stays the same while the payment method changes. These products are live in market today, so the question for issuers is whether they’re positioned to deliver one.

Why consumers want them

Interest is strongest among younger consumers: 48% of 18 to 44 year olds are interested, and 60% of 18 to 34 year olds started their financial journey with a credit product, which makes them more attuned to flexibility. Consumers say they want to:

Use the right payment method for each purchase without carrying multiple cards

Access BNPL for larger purchases without opening a separate account

Manage cash flow at the point of sale, not after the fact

Avoid managing multiple provider relationships

Notably, 71% of consumers with multiple credit cards want to switch between credit products at checkout. They already have the products but can’t use them fluidly in one transaction.

The cost of not delivering

Consumers switch providers because of improved credit scores, life changes, or better rewards elsewhere, not because something went wrong. Providers won’t lose customers in a dramatic moment. They’ll lose them gradually, one contextual payment decision at a time, as customers reach for a different card when theirs can’t do what’s needed. With flexible credentials increasingly visible on social feeds, through peers, and at checkout, that moment is coming soon. With a flexible credential, the relationship deepens rather than fragments.

Marqeta platform data shows the shift is underway: through the first five months of 2025, BNPL average order values fell 9% year over year, while non-discretionary spend TPV rose more than 60% from 2023 to 2024. Consumers are folding BNPL into everyday spending.

The SMB opportunity

60% of SMBs are interested in flexible payment orchestration, with interest rising among growth-stage businesses. A single card that can pay a supplier on net terms, split an equipment purchase into installments, and draw on credit for operating expenses offers something no static card can. SMBs represent one of the largest untapped opportunities in credit today.

What issuers need to get right

The question isn’t whether to offer flexible credentials but when, and on what infrastructure. Providers that move now will win customers actively looking for this product, while those that wait will find them locked in with faster competitors.

Infrastructure: A platform that handles multiple payment types, real-time decisioning, and dynamic credential switching through a single API. Stitching together separate debit, credit, and BNPL point solutions won’t deliver the seamless experience consumers expect.

The credit product underneath: Programmable credit infrastructure that lets program managers set their own approval models, limits, and terms.

The consumer experience: Switching at checkout must be effortless, or the experience fails regardless of the infrastructure.

The bottom line

When 67% of consumers say they’d replace their primary debit card, they’re describing a product they’d adopt from a provider they already trust. Those who respond with the right product on the right infrastructure will hold a durable advantage in consumer and SMB credit for the next decade.

title: New payment rails catch on, slowly
snippet: Some companies have yet to realize the full potential of multi-rail systems, speakers said at the Money20/20 conference said Monday.
fullText:
Companies have presided over big shifts in money flows in recent years as technology has transformed transactions. 

Yet speakers at a conference Monday said financial institutions and other businesses will need to overcome more hurdles if they want to realize all of the benefits of instant payments and stablecoins for payment senders and receivers. 

“At the end of the day our customers and their customers are counting on us, they don’t care about the rails, they don’t care about the modality,” Amy Burr, chief product and relationship officer with Federal Reserve Financial Services, said during a panel at the Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas. “They want to know that money is going to move reliably, quickly and independently; the end. That’s the challenge and we need to rise up and meet it.” 

To be sure, businesses are making inroads into new systems. Consumer card-swiping, digital wallets and an ever widening range of corporate payment methods have been part of the transformation of economic exchanges that has driven annual global payments revenue from $1.7 trillion in 2020 to $2.6 trillion last year, according to the consulting firm McKinsey.  

Still, skepticism and old technology are holding some companies and banks back from full adoption of the wider range of alternative forms of the payments — ranging from stablecoins to the Federal Reserve’s instant payment system, FedNow — as well as the benefits that modern payments technology can offer. 

“I spend a fair amount of time talking to financial institutions that just don’t want another thing,” Burr said during the panel discussion at the  conference, noting that some companies are reluctant to add more layers to their technology stack. “The fatigue is real.”

The ideal of a fully activated modernized payments ecosystem and how companies can take steps to surmount the hurdles that are still preventing it from being realized, was the focus of a panel discussion at the annual finance and technology conference.

Burr expressed some skepticism about the uptake of the new technologies because of the relatively lukewarm reception that banks gave to a new international standard known as ISO 20022. The Fedwire Funds Service, which moves trillions of dollars daily, shifted to the standard last year, but banks are just beginning to embrace it and make use of its attributes. 

While there’s been effort to push adoption of the full benefit of ISO 20022, “we’re not really seeing banks and corporates using all the fields so I’m maybe a little pessimistic about programmable money,” Burr said. 

Sam Aarons, CTO of payments software provider Modern Treasury, said he is frustrated personally by capabilities for payments, some of which would make them more user-friendly, but which aren’t being widely adopted. For example, he said he can log into his credit card account and see purchases, but receipts are not included — even though technology can provide that capability and allow card users to have more information about their purchases.  

“It irks me to no end that I can’t log into my American Express portal and see the receipt attached to my payment,” Aarons said, noting that he believes the problem is likely tied to decades old software that hasn’t caught up with technology. “We have all this innovation for stapling context data to payments, and still no one does it.” 

As companies explore their payment system options, Aarons advised that they think about payments rails as a kind of menu, with paths that might or might not fit their needs at a given time. That includes keeping some existing rails operating, such as ACH payments, that some companies like for their low cost, and even paper checks. 

“You still see paper checks; they’re very popular in the United States,” Aarons said. “The volume will get reduced over the years but not to zero.” 

Currently, he said big companies are not viewing stablecoins versus fiat currency as an either or question but are rather using all of them in varied degrees depending on their needs. 

Irfan Ganchi, senior vice president of product management at stablecoin giant Circle Internet Group, agreed. The choice of how the money gets to a place is something that depends on the location of the receivers and senders, as well as the capabilities of the rails, he said. For example, Ganchi said large multinational companies may use stablecoin to move a payment to some of their international entities overnight, but locally they’re going to pay local suppliers and vendors using instant payments. 

“But also there’s an aspect of receiver preference,” he said. “It’s quite possible that a ride sharing driver in Indonesia wants [Circle’s stablecoin] USDC because they want to hold it in dollars. But a ride sharing driver in the U.S. wants dollars or fiat and you have to be able to support both.”  

The Money20/20 conference is owned by Payment Dive’s parent company Informa.

title: PayPal isn’t agile enough, CEO says
snippet: As part of his turnaround efforts, Enrique Lores said Monday the digital payments company requires faster decisions and clearer accountability.
fullText:
PayPal Holdings was slow to make decisions under its prior leadership, with too many management layers bogging down the pace of execution, Chief Executive Enrique Lores said Monday during a discussion at an industry conference.

The digital payments company needs to “simplify how we work, remove (and) accelerate decision makers, reduce management layers, and become a more agile company,” Lores said on stage during a conversation about his turnaround plans for PayPal at the annual Money 20/20 financial technology conference.

“We have clarified how decisions need to be made and clarified accountability,” said Lores, who was PayPal’s chairman before assuming the CEO role on March 1 after Alex Chriss exited. “And having been in business for a long time, I know accountability is one of the most important things to improve performance.”

Lores offered a brief summary of some of PayPal’s past faults during the discussion, explaining his strategy for the company’s turnaround. He spoke with Karen Webster, the chief executive of PYMNTS, a business-to-business publisher.

PayPal’s Venmo peer-to-peer fund transfer service and the Braintree processing system “were not getting enough attention, were not getting enough investment, and we have changed that,” Lores said.

As part of the turnaround, the company has begun cutting jobs, but has not specified the size of the reductions envisioned under Lores’ three-year plan. Bloomberg and the Wall Street Journal reported in May that PayPal aims to reduce its global workforce by about 20% over the restructuring period, citing people familiar with the plans.

San Jose, California-based PayPal also reportedly assessed a potential sale of the business to digital processing peer Stripe and private equity firm Advent International after they made a bid for the company in July. But the suitors abandoned that effort the following month, Bloomberg reported.

Lores did not discuss the sale discussions or the scope of job cuts during his remarks Monday on the second day of the event in Las Vegas

Under Lores, PayPal is betting that a focus on consumer financial services, such as buy now pay later, personal banking and Venmo payments will spark growth and lift its laggard stock price, which has declined about 76% over the past five years.

“The attention of the company has been much more in the merchant side than in the consumer side,” he said. “And we are revitalizing what we do for consumers, understanding better what our consumers do, and shaping our portfolio for them.” 

PayPal also intends to leverage its brand trust with merchants and consumers to capitalize on the expected boom of agentic commerce transactions conducted with consumers’ personal agents, he said. 

“Trust was very important when e-commerce started,” Lores said, referencing the company’s roots as an early digital player. “It’s going to be even more important in an agentic world, and that’s the position that we need to occupy.”

PayPal doesn’t expect any meaningful sales volumes from agentic commerce until 2028, Lores said, although the company is investing in infrastructure and partnerships to prepare for that growth. “If we are realistic, the amount of commerce that is done through agents in ‘26, or that will be done in ‘27, is going to be relatively small,” he said.

PayPal has learned that its most engaged and valuable customers “really would like us to offer a broader portfolio of financial services,” the CEO said.

PayPal’s push into more consumer finance “doesn't mean that we are going to be abandoning checkout,” he said. “Checkout will continue to be very relevant, but we have complemented it with an additional portfolio of services.”

PayPal is also using the turnaround effort as an opportunity to modernize its internal technology stack, with artificial intelligence helping to accelerate that process, Lores said. “We can do in the next 18 months things that in the past would have taken us three or four years,” he said.

title: Visa, Mastercard urge court to approve fee settlement
snippet: The card networks contend Walmart and trade groups want to scuttle a legal pact over card swipe fees using recycled arguments the court has rejected.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

The card networks contend Walmart and trade groups want to scuttle a legal pact over card swipe fees using recycled arguments the court has rejected.

        

            

        Published Oct. 16, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                A federal judge in Brooklyn, New York will convene a hearing next month to weigh final approval of a settlement between a class of 12 million merchants and card networks Visa and Mastercard.
            
        
            Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Visa and Mastercard contended in a court filing this week that merchants seeking to derail approval of a legal settlement over card swipe fees are recycling arguments they’ve made previously, and that the court has rejected. Some of the plaintiffs also have overestimated their prospects of winning at a trial, the card networks said.

Even if merchants were to win the case, “it remains unlikely that the Court would order remedies anywhere near as extreme as those the objectors claim they want, particularly given their harmful effects on cardholders and on internetwork competition,” Visa and Mastercard attorneys wrote Wednesday in a joint reply to objections lodged against the pact. The filing comes a month before a federal judge plans to hold a final approval hearing on Nov. 16.

The card networks also told the court that several large trade associations and Walmart “constitute no more than a vocal minority objecting to the settlement,” given the class size of more than 12 million members. “It is now clear that the concerns raised at preliminary approval and reiterated by largely the same objectors at final approval are nowhere near ‘pervasive,’” the companies wrote.

Dive Insight:

“Rather than offering any factual or legal basis why the Court should revisit and reverse its findings at preliminary approval, the objections merely reprise the same arguments this Court already considered and rejected,” Visa and Mastercard wrote in their support of final court approval.

The class counsel representing merchants also filed their reply to the merchants’ objections, on Wednesday, but they did so under seal. U.S. District Judge Brian Cogan told the lawyers to articulate by Monday proposed redactions to the filing so he could assess any need for confidentiality against the right of public access.

The class lawyers and networks’ attorneys reached the proposed settlement a year ago, with Cogan granting it preliminary approval in June, finding it superior to a 2024 settlement the court rejected. The litigation dates to 2005.

The latest settlement would trim credit interchange rates by 10 basis points for five years and impose a 1.25% rate for standard consumer cards for eight years. It would also give merchants the right to decline some higher-cost branded Visa and Mastercard premium and commercial credit cards. That would be a departure from the networks’ “honor all cards” rule requiring merchants to accept all cards from the networks if they accept any cards. 

In 2024, merchants paid a 2.35% fee, on average, on Visa and Mastercard transactions, according to industry research organization Nilson Report last year.

Merchants would also gain new rights to add surcharges and offer discounts for cards as a way to steer customers away from cards with higher interchange fees. But large merchants argued that they can’t easily reject the premium cards issued by banks – which offer consumers travel and cashback rewards and carry higher fees – because they are popular with customers.

The card networks also contended that objections from the National Retail Federation and Retail Industry Leaders Associations should be discounted due to several of their member companies supporting the settlement.

“Given this context, the trade association objections should be afforded little (if any) weight, and the Court should not accept the implication that those objections reflect the views of the associations’ individual members,” Visa and Mastercard wrote.

If a trial were to move forward, the merchants would likely lose given the networks’ various arguments, Visa and Mastercard told the court. “The obstacles to achieving objectors’ preferred trial result are further compounded by the complexity of this case and the certainty that appellate litigation would follow from any judgment in favor of the class,” they said.

They also urged the court to reject Walmart’s “novel proposition” that the retailer should be allowed to opt out of the class because its inclusion constitutes an unjust taking of a legal claim.

Separately, the plaintiffs’ counsel filed an objection Thursday to a request for $36 million in legal fees from 18 merchant-plaintiffs who settled for damages from the networks in a related case over swipe fees.

That group of merchants – including Crate & Barrel Holdings, Dick’s Sporting Goods, The Gap and Yum! Brands – asked the court last month for “objector fees” for their role in helping to gain improvements for merchants between the current settlement and the one reached two years ago.

If granted, the fee award would reduce the class counsel’s proposed fees to $170 million for their work in the case.
